title: Part 1, Chapter 45
paragraphs: In which the doubtful question of Mambrino's helmet and the pack-saddle is finally settled, with other adventures that occurred in truth and earnest
"What do you all think now, gentlemen," said the barber, "of what these fine gentlemen are saying when they try to make out that this is a helmet?"
"And anyone who says the opposite," said Don Quixote, "I'll let him know he lies — if he's a knight; and if he's a squire, that he lies a thousand times over."

Our own barber, who had been present through all of this and understood Don Quixote's brand of madness perfectly, decided to back up the delusion and keep the joke going for everyone's amusement; so turning to the other barber he said:

"Señor barber, or whatever you are, you should know that I belong to your profession too. I've held a licence to practise for more than twenty years, and I know every implement of the barber's craft inside out. I was also a soldier for a time in my youth, so I know what a helmet is, and a morion, and a headpiece with a visor, and the other gear of soldiering — I mean to say, of soldiers' arms. And I say — saving better opinions and always deferring to sounder judgments — that this piece in front of us, which this worthy gentleman has in his hands, not only is not a barber's basin, but is as far from being one as white is from black, or truth from falsehood. I'll add that this, although it is a helmet, is not a complete helmet."
"Certainly not," said Don Quixote, "because half of it is missing — the beaver, that is."

"Quite true," said the curate, who could see what his friend the barber was up to. Cardenio, Don Fernando, and his companions agreed, and even the Judge would have helped carry on the joke if his mind hadn't been so occupied with Don Luis's situation; but the serious matter weighing on him left him paying little or no attention to these comic proceedings.

"God help me!" exclaimed the barber, the butt of all this. "Is it possible that such an honourable company can say this is not a basin but a helmet? Why, this would astonish an entire university, however learned. Enough — if this basin is a helmet, then the pack-saddle must be a horse's caparison, as this gentleman has said."
"To me it looks like a pack-saddle," said Don Quixote, "but I've already said I will not get involved in that question."
"Whether it's a pack-saddle or a caparison," said the curate, "is for Señor Don Quixote to decide; for in matters of chivalry all of us gentlemen bow to his authority."

"By God, gentlemen," said Don Quixote, "so many strange things have happened to me in this castle during the two visits I've made that I won't venture to assert anything positively about anything in it. It's my belief that everything that goes on here happens by enchantment. The first time, an enchanted Moor who lives here gave me a great deal of trouble, and Sancho didn't fare well with certain followers of his either. And last night I was left hanging by this arm for nearly two hours, with no idea how or why such a thing came to pass. So for me to step forward now and give an opinion on so puzzling a matter would be reckless. As for the claim that this is a basin and not a helmet, I've already answered. But on the question of whether this is a pack-saddle or a caparison, I won't venture a firm opinion — I'll leave it to your worships' better judgment. Perhaps, since you've not been dubbed knights as I have, the enchantments of this place have no hold on you, your faculties are unfettered, and you can see things in this castle as they really and truly are, rather than as they appear to me."

"There can be no question," said Don Fernando, "that Señor Don Quixote has spoken very wisely, and that the decision rests with us. And so we may have surer ground to go on, I'll take the gentlemen's votes in secret and announce the result clearly and fully."

To those who were in on the joke about Don Quixote's mania this was all great fun, but to those who knew nothing about it, it seemed the most absurd nonsense in the world — particularly to Don Luis's four servants, to Don Luis himself, and to three other travellers who had chanced to arrive at the inn and looked like officers of the Holy Brotherhood, which is in fact what they were. But the one who was most at his wits' end was the barber whose basin, in front of his very eyes, had turned into Mambrino's helmet, and whose pack-saddle, he had no doubt, was about to become a rich horse's caparison. Everyone laughed to see Don Fernando going from one to another collecting votes and whispering to them to give their private opinion on whether the much-fought-over treasure was a pack-saddle or a caparison. After he had taken the votes of those who knew Don Quixote, he said aloud, "The fact is, my good fellow, I'm tired of collecting opinions, because there isn't one of those I've asked who doesn't tell me it's absurd to say this is the pack-saddle of an ass and not the caparison of a horse — indeed, of a thoroughbred horse. So you'll have to submit; for, in spite of you and your ass, this is a caparison and no pack-saddle, and you have stated and proved your case very poorly."

"May I never see heaven," said the poor barber, "if your worships aren't all mistaken. May my soul appear before God just as that thing appears to me to be a pack-saddle and not a caparison. But — 'laws go as kings like' — I'll say no more. And no, I'm not drunk: I'm fasting, except from sin."
The barber's simple talk was no less amusing than Don Quixote's absurdities, and Don Quixote now observed:
"There's nothing more to be done now than for each man to take what belongs to him, and to whom God has given it, may St. Peter add his blessing."

But one of the four servants said, "Unless this is a deliberate joke, I cannot bring myself to believe that men as intelligent as those here are, or appear to be, would dare declare and assert that this is not a basin and that not a pack-saddle. But since I see they are declaring it, I can only conclude there's some mystery in their insisting on what so plainly contradicts experience and the truth itself. By" — and here he let out a round oath — "all the people in the world won't make me believe that this is not a barber's basin and that not a jackass's pack-saddle."
"It might just as easily be a she-ass's," observed the curate.
"It's all the same," said the servant. "That's not the point. The point is whether it is or isn't a pack-saddle, as your worships are saying."

Hearing this, one of the newly arrived officers of the Brotherhood, who had been listening to the dispute, lost his patience and exclaimed, "It is a pack-saddle, as sure as my father is my father, and whoever has said or will say anything else must be drunk."

"You lie like a rascally clown," Don Quixote shot back; and lifting his pike, which he had never let out of his hand, he aimed such a blow at the man's head that, had the officer not dodged it, he would have been laid out flat. The pike shattered against the ground. The rest of the officers, seeing their comrade attacked, raised a shout calling for help for the Holy Brotherhood. The landlord, who was a member of the fraternity, ran at once to fetch his staff of office and his sword and lined up with his comrades. Don Luis's servants clustered around him so he couldn't slip away in the confusion. The barber, seeing the house in uproar, grabbed his pack-saddle again, and Sancho did the same. Don Quixote drew his sword and charged the officers. Don Luis was shouting at his servants to leave him alone and go help Don Quixote, while Cardenio and Don Fernando backed Don Quixote up. The curate was yelling at the top of his lungs, the landlady screaming, her daughter wailing, Maritornes weeping, Dorothea aghast, Luscinda terror-stricken, and Doña Clara in a faint. The barber clubbed Sancho, and Sancho pummelled the barber. Don Luis gave one of his servants — who had grabbed his arm to keep him from escaping — a clout that bloodied his teeth. The Judge took his part. Don Fernando had one of the officers on the ground and was thrashing him soundly. The landlord shouted again for help for the Holy Brotherhood. The whole inn was nothing but cries, shouts, shrieks, confusion, terror, dismay, mishaps, sword-cuts, fisticuffs, cudgellings, kicks, and bloodshed. And in the middle of all this chaos and tangle, Don Quixote took it into his head that he had been dropped right into the thick of the discord of Agramante's camp; and in a voice that shook the inn like thunder he cried out:
"Stop, everyone! Let everyone sheathe his sword, let everyone be calm and listen to me, as you value your lives!"

Everyone paused at the force of his voice, and he went on, "Did I not tell you, sirs, that this castle was enchanted, and that a legion of devils dwelt in it? As proof I call on you to see with your own eyes how the discord of Agramante's camp has come here and been transferred into the middle of us. Look how they fight — there for the sword, here for the horse, over there for the eagle, on this side for the helmet; we are all fighting, and all at cross purposes. Come then, you, Señor Judge, and you, señor curate — let the one stand as King Agramante and the other as King Sobrino, and make peace among us. By God Almighty, it is a sorry thing that so many people of quality as we are should kill one another over such trifles." The officers, who did not understand Don Quixote's manner of speaking and found themselves roughly handled by Don Fernando, Cardenio, and their companions, were not about to be appeased. The barber was, however, since both his beard and his pack-saddle were the worse for the struggle. Sancho, like a good servant, obeyed his master's slightest word, while Don Luis's four servants kept quiet when they saw how little they gained by being otherwise. The landlord alone insisted they must punish the insolence of this madman, who at every turn raised an uproar in the inn. But at length the disturbance was stilled for the time being. In Don Quixote's imagination the pack-saddle remained a caparison until the day of judgment, the basin a helmet, and the inn a castle.

Once everyone had been calmed and reconciled by the Judge's and the curate's persuasion, Don Luis's servants began again to press him to return home with them at once. While he was arguing with them, the Judge took counsel with Don Fernando, Cardenio, and the curate about what he should do, telling them how things stood and what Don Luis had said to him. It was finally agreed that Don Fernando would tell Don Luis's servants who he was, and that it was his wish that Don Luis accompany him to Andalusia, where Don Luis would receive from his brother the marquis the welcome his rank deserved; for otherwise it was clear from Don Luis's determination that he wouldn't return to his father right now, even if they tore him to pieces. On learning Don Fernando's rank and Don Luis's resolve, the four settled it among themselves: three of them would go back to tell his father how matters stood, and the fourth would stay to wait on Don Luis and not leave him until they returned to fetch him or his father's orders arrived. So by the authority of Agramante and the wisdom of King Sobrino this whole tangle of disputes was arranged. But the enemy of concord and hater of peace, feeling himself slighted and made a fool of, and seeing how little he'd gained after weaving them all into so elaborate an entanglement, resolved to try his hand once more by stirring up fresh quarrels and disturbances.

It came about this way. The officers were pacified once they learned the rank of those they'd been fighting, and withdrew from the contest, judging that whatever the outcome they were likely to come off the worse. But one of them — the one Don Fernando had thrashed and kicked — remembered that among the warrants he carried for the arrest of various criminals he had one against Don Quixote, whom the Holy Brotherhood had ordered arrested for freeing the galley slaves, exactly as Sancho had very reasonably feared. Suspecting this, he wanted to confirm whether Don Quixote's features matched the description. Taking a parchment out of his coat, he found what he was looking for, and setting himself to read it slowly — because he was no quick reader — he fixed his eyes on Don Quixote with each word, comparing the description in the warrant with his face, and concluded that beyond any doubt this was the man named in it. Once satisfied, he folded up the parchment, took the warrant in his left hand, and with his right grabbed Don Quixote by the collar so tightly that he could hardly breathe, and shouted, "Help for the Holy Brotherhood! And to show you I'm serious, read this warrant, which says this highwayman is to be arrested."

The curate took the warrant and saw that what the officer said was true, and that it matched Don Quixote's appearance. Don Quixote, finding himself roughly handled by this rascally clown, was worked up to the highest pitch of fury, every joint cracking with rage. With both hands he seized the officer by the throat with all his strength, so that had his comrades not come to his aid he would have given up his life before Don Quixote let go. The landlord, who was bound to support his fellow officers, ran at once to help them. The landlady, seeing her husband caught up in yet another fight, again raised her voice, and Maritornes and the daughter immediately joined her, calling on heaven and everyone present for help. Sancho, watching all this, exclaimed, "By the Lord, what my master says about the enchantments of this castle is true — it's impossible to live an hour in peace here!"

Don Fernando separated the officer and Don Quixote, and to their mutual relief made them release their grip — the one on the coat collar, the other on his adversary's throat. Even so, the officers did not stop demanding their prisoner and calling on the others to help them and hand him over bound, as was required for the service of the King and of the Holy Brotherhood, on whose behalf they once more demanded aid in capturing this robber and footpad of the highways.

Don Quixote smiled when he heard these words and said very calmly, "Come now, you base, ill-born brood — do you call it highway robbery to give freedom to those in bondage, to release captives, to help the wretched, to raise up the fallen, to relieve the needy? You infamous creatures, whose vile, grovelling intellects deserve that heaven should never reveal to you the virtue that lies in knight-errantry, nor show you the sin and ignorance in which you wallow when you refuse to respect even the shadow, let alone the presence, of any knight-errant. Come on then — band, not of officers, but of thieves, footpads licensed by the Holy Brotherhood: tell me, who was the fool that signed an arrest warrant against such a knight as I am? Who didn't know that knights-errant are independent of all jurisdictions, that their law is their sword, their charter their prowess, and their edicts their will? Who, I ask again, was the dolt who doesn't know that there are no patents of nobility that confer such privileges or exemptions as a knight-errant acquires the day he is dubbed and devotes himself to the demanding calling of chivalry? What knight-errant ever paid poll-tax, duty, queen's pin-money, king's dues, toll, or ferry? What tailor ever made him pay for his clothes? What castellan who received him in his castle ever made him pay his bill? What king did not seat him at his table? What damsel did not fall in love with him and surrender herself wholly to his will and pleasure? And finally, what knight-errant has there ever been, or is there, or will there ever be in the world who isn't bold enough single-handedly to give four hundred cudgellings to four hundred officers of the Holy Brotherhood if they cross his path?"

title: Part 1, Chapter 46
paragraphs: About the end of the notable adventure of the officers of the Holy Brotherhood; and the great ferocity of our worthy knight, Don Quixote

While Don Quixote was carrying on like this, the curate was trying to convince the officers that he was out of his mind, as they could see from his actions and his words, and that they need not press the matter — even if they arrested him and took him away, they'd have to release him before long as a madman. The officer holding the warrant replied that it was not his business to investigate Don Quixote's madness, only to carry out his superior's orders, and that once he had him in custody they could let him go three hundred times if they pleased.
"All the same," said the curate, "you mustn't take him away this time, and in my opinion he won't let himself be taken either."

In the end the curate argued so well, and Don Quixote did such mad things, that the officers would have been madder than he was if they hadn't recognised his lack of wits; so they thought it best to be pacified, and even to act as peacemakers between the barber and Sancho Panza, who were still bitterly arguing. In the end the officers, in their capacity as officers of justice, settled the matter by arbitration in such a way that both sides were, if not perfectly contented, at least somewhat satisfied: they swapped the pack-saddles but not the girths or head-stalls. As for Mambrino's helmet, the curate, on the quiet and without Don Quixote knowing, paid eight reals for the basin, and the barber wrote out a full receipt and an undertaking to make no further demand then or thereafter, forever, amen. With these two disputes — the most important — settled, all that remained was for Don Luis's servants to agree that three of them would go back while one stayed to accompany him wherever Don Fernando wanted to take him. Good luck and better fortune, having already begun to clear away difficulties and remove obstacles in favour of the lovers and warriors at the inn, were pleased to keep going and bring everything to a happy resolution: the servants agreed to do as Don Luis wished, which gave Doña Clara such happiness that no one could have looked into her face at that moment without seeing the joy in her heart. Zoraida, though she didn't fully understand all she was seeing, was grave or cheerful without knowing why, as she watched and studied the various faces — especially her Spaniard's, whom she followed with her eyes and clung to with her soul. The gift and compensation the curate had given the barber hadn't escaped the landlord's notice, and he demanded payment of Don Quixote's reckoning, plus the cost of the damage to his wine-skins and the loss of his wine, swearing that neither Rocinante nor Sancho's ass would leave the inn until he'd been paid down to the last farthing. The curate settled it all amicably, and Don Fernando paid — though the Judge had also been very ready to settle the bill. Everything became so peaceful and quiet that the inn no longer brought to mind the discord of Agramante's camp, as Don Quixote had put it, but the peace and tranquillity of the days of Octavianus. The universal opinion was that thanks were due to the great zeal and eloquence of the curate, and to the unexampled generosity of Don Fernando.

Now that he was clear of all quarrels — his squire's as well as his own — Don Quixote considered it would be wise to resume the journey he'd begun and bring to a close that great adventure for which he had been called and chosen. With this lofty resolve he went and knelt before Dorothea, who refused to let him say a word until he had risen; so to obey her he stood up and said, "There's a common proverb, fair lady, that 'diligence is the mother of good fortune,' and experience has often shown in important matters that the persistence of the negotiator brings a doubtful case to a successful end. But nowhere does this truth show itself more plainly than in war, where speed and decisiveness anticipate the enemy's schemes and win the victory before the foe has time to defend himself. I say all this, exalted and esteemed lady, because it seems to me that for us to remain any longer in this castle is useless now, and may yet prove harmful in some way we'll find out one day. Who's to say your enemy the giant has not learned by means of secret and diligent spies that I am going to destroy him? And if the chance is given him, he may take it to fortify himself in some impregnable castle or stronghold against which all my efforts and the might of my tireless arm might avail very little. So, lady, let us, as I say, forestall his schemes by our quickness, and depart at once in quest of fair fortune. Your highness is only being kept from enjoying it as fully as you'd wish by my delay in confronting your adversary."

Don Quixote fell silent and waited calmly for the beautiful princess's reply. With commanding dignity and in a style adapted to Don Quixote's own, she answered, "I thank you, sir knight, for the eagerness you show — like the good knight you are, to whom it's a natural obligation to help the orphan and the needy — to come to my aid in my sore trouble. And heaven grant that your wishes and mine may be fulfilled, so you may see there are women in this world capable of gratitude. As for my departure, let it be at once, for I have no will but yours. Dispose of me entirely as you see fit. She who has once entrusted to you the defence of her person, and placed in your hands the recovery of her kingdom, must not think of offering opposition to whatever your wisdom may decree."

"On then, in God's name," said Don Quixote, "for when a lady humbles herself to me, I will not miss the chance to raise her up and set her on the throne of her ancestors. Let us depart at once. The common saying that 'in delay there is danger' lends spurs to my eagerness to take the road. Since neither heaven has created nor hell has seen anything that can daunt or intimidate me, saddle Rocinante, Sancho, and get ready your ass and the queen's palfrey, and let us take leave of the castellan and these gentlemen and go this very instant."
Sancho, who had been standing by the whole time, said, shaking his head, "Oh, master, master, there's more mischief afoot in the village than gets talked about — saving the pardon of all good folk."
"What mischief can there be in any village, or in all the cities of the world, you booby, that can damage my reputation?" said Don Quixote.
"If your worship's getting angry," Sancho replied, "I'll hold my tongue and leave unsaid what a good squire is bound to say, and what a good servant should tell his master."

"Say what you like," Don Quixote returned, "so long as your words aren't meant to work on my fears. If you're afraid, you're behaving like yourself; but I'm behaving like myself, in not being afraid."

"It's nothing of the sort, as I'm a sinner before God," said Sancho, "but I take it as sure and certain that this lady, who calls herself queen of the great kingdom of Micomicón, is no more queen than my mother. If she were what she says, she wouldn't go rubbing noses every minute with a certain someone here behind every door."

Dorothea turned red at Sancho's words, because the truth was her husband Don Fernando had now and then, when others weren't looking, gathered from her lips some of the reward his love had earned, and Sancho, seeing this, had concluded that such liberties were more suited to a courtesan than to the queen of a great kingdom. Unable, or unwilling, to answer him, she let him go on, and he continued, "I say this, señor, because if after we've travelled roads and highways, gone through bad nights and worse days, one who's now enjoying himself in this inn is to reap the fruit of our labour, there's no rush for me to saddle Rocinante, put the pad on the ass, or get the palfrey ready. Better for us to stay put, and let every jade mind her spinning, and let's go to dinner."

Good God, what was Don Quixote's outrage when he heard his squire's brazen words! So great that, in a voice strangled with rage, his tongue stammering and his eyes flashing live fire, he exclaimed, "Rascally clown, boorish, insolent, ignorant, foul-mouthed, impudent backbiter and slanderer! How dare you utter such words in my presence and that of these noble ladies? How dare you harbour such gross and shameless thoughts in your muddled imagination? Get out of my sight, you born monster, storehouse of lies, hoard of untruths, granary of dirty tricks, inventor of scandals, broadcaster of absurdities, enemy of the respect due to royal persons! Get out, and don't appear before me again on pain of my fury." Saying this, he knitted his brows, puffed out his cheeks, glared around him, and stamped his right foot violently on the ground, displaying in every way the rage pent up in his heart. At his words and furious gestures Sancho was so terrified that he would have been glad if the earth had opened on the spot and swallowed him, and his only thought was to turn and bolt from the angry presence of his master.

But the quick-witted Dorothea, by now thoroughly familiar with Don Quixote's habit of mind, said, to soothe his wrath, "Don't be irritated, Knight of the Rueful Countenance, at the absurdities your good squire has uttered. Perhaps he didn't speak without cause; given his good sense and Christian conscience, it's unlikely he'd bear false witness against anyone. We may therefore believe, without hesitation, that since — as you yourself say, sir knight — everything in this castle goes on by means of enchantment, Sancho may well have seen, through this diabolical medium, what he claims to have seen, so much to the detriment of my modesty."

"I swear by God Almighty," exclaimed Don Quixote, "your highness has hit the mark; some vile illusion must have appeared before this sinner of a Sancho that made him see what couldn't otherwise be seen except by enchantment. I know perfectly well, from the poor fellow's goodness and harmlessness, that he is incapable of bearing false witness against anybody."

"True, no doubt," said Don Fernando, "and for that reason, Señor Don Quixote, you ought to forgive him and restore him to the bosom of your favour, _sicut erat in principio_, before illusions of this kind had taken away his senses."

Don Quixote said he was ready to pardon him, and the curate went to fetch Sancho, who came in very meekly, fell on his knees, and begged for his master's hand. Don Quixote gave it to him, allowed him to kiss it, then gave him his blessing and said, "Now, Sancho my son, you'll be convinced of the truth of what I have told you so often — that everything in this castle is done by enchantment."
"So I believe," said Sancho, "except the business of the blanket, which really happened by ordinary means."

"Don't believe it," said Don Quixote, "for if it had been so, I would have avenged you that instant, or even now; but neither then nor now could I, and I have not seen anyone on whom to avenge your wrong."

They were all curious to know what the blanket business was, and the landlord gave them a detailed account of Sancho's flights through the air, at which they laughed a great deal. Sancho would have been just as embarrassed if his master hadn't once more assured him it was all enchantment. For all that, his simple-mindedness never reached such a pitch that he could convince himself it wasn't the plain and simple truth, without any deception about it, that he'd been blanketed by beings of flesh and blood and not by visionary, imaginary phantoms, as his master believed and insisted.

The illustrious company had now been two days at the inn, and as it seemed time to leave, they devised a plan so that, without putting Dorothea and Don Fernando to the trouble of going back with Don Quixote to his village under pretext of restoring Queen Micomicona, the curate and the barber might carry him off with them as they had proposed, and the curate could try to take his madness in hand at home. To put the plan into action, they arranged with the owner of an ox-cart who happened to be passing to carry Don Quixote as follows. They built a kind of cage of wooden bars, big enough to hold him comfortably. Then Don Fernando and his companions, Don Luis's servants, and the officers of the Brotherhood, together with the landlord, all under the curate's directions, covered their faces and disguised themselves in various ways so as to appear to Don Quixote completely different from the people he had seen in the castle. This done, in complete silence they entered the room where he was asleep, resting from his recent scuffles. They moved up to where he lay tranquilly, not dreaming of any such thing, seized him firmly, and bound him fast hand and foot. When he woke up with a start he couldn't move, and could only marvel and wonder at the strange figures before him. He immediately gave way to the idea his crazed imagination always conjured up: he took it that all these shapes were phantoms of the enchanted castle, and that he himself was unquestionably enchanted, since he could neither move nor help himself — which was exactly what the curate, who had cooked up the scheme, expected. Of all those present, Sancho was the only one in his senses and his own proper character; and although he was within a hair's breadth of sharing his master's affliction, he did not fail to recognise who all these disguised figures were. But he didn't dare open his mouth until he saw what would come of this assault and capture of his master; and Don Quixote also said nothing, waiting to see how his predicament would end. The outcome was that they brought in the cage, shut him up in it, and nailed the bars so firmly they couldn't easily be broken open.

They then lifted him onto their shoulders, and as they were carrying him out of the room a terrifying voice — as terrifying as the barber (not the one of the pack-saddle but the other) could make it — was heard to say, "O Knight of the Rueful Countenance, let not this captivity in which thou art placed afflict thee; for thus must it be, for the speedier accomplishment of the adventure in which thy great heart hath engaged thee. The same shall be accomplished when the raging Manchegan lion and the white Tobosan dove shall be joined together, having first humbled their haughty necks to the gentle yoke of matrimony. And from this marvellous union there shall come forth into the light of the world brave whelps that shall rival the ravening claws of their valiant father; and this shall come to pass before the pursuer of the flying nymph hath, in his swift natural course, twice visited the starry signs. And thou, O most noble and obedient squire that ever bore sword at side, beard on face, or nose to smell with, be not dismayed or grieved to see the flower of knight-errantry carried off thus before thy very eyes; for soon, if it please the Framer of the universe, thou shalt see thyself raised to such a height that thou shalt not know thyself, and the promises thy good master hath made thee shall not prove false. And I assure thee, on the authority of the sage Mentironiana, that thy wages shall be paid thee, as thou shalt see in due season. Follow then in the footsteps of the valiant enchanted knight, for it is fitting that thou shouldst go to the destination assigned to you both; and as it is not permitted to me to say more, God be with thee, for I now return to that place I wot of." As he brought the prophecy to a close he raised his voice to a high pitch and then lowered it to such a soft tone that even those who knew it was all a joke were almost tempted to take what they heard seriously.

Don Quixote was greatly comforted by the prophecy, for he understood its meaning at once and perceived it was promising him that he would see himself united in holy and lawful matrimony with his beloved Dulcinea del Toboso, from whose blessed womb would come forth the whelps — his sons — to the eternal glory of La Mancha. Thoroughly and firmly persuaded of this, he raised his voice and with a deep sigh exclaimed, "O you, whoever you are, who have foretold so much good to me, I beg you, on my behalf, to entreat the sage enchanter who looks after my interests not to let me perish in this captivity in which they're now carrying me away before I see fulfilled such joyful and incomparable promises as those that have now been made to me. Let this only come to pass and I shall glory in the pains of my prison, find comfort in these chains they bind me with, and regard this bed they stretch me on, not as a hard battlefield, but as a soft and happy nuptial couch. And as for the consolation of Sancho Panza, my squire, I rely on his goodness and integrity not to desert me in good fortune or bad. If, by his ill luck or mine, it should not be in my power to give him the island I promised him, or some equivalent, at least his wages shall not be lost; for in my will, which is already drawn up, I have set down the sum to be paid him — measured not by his many faithful services but by the means at my disposal."

Sancho bowed his head very respectfully and kissed both his master's hands, for, being tied together, he could not kiss one. Then the apparitions hoisted the cage onto their shoulders and set it upon the ox-cart.

title: Part 1, Chapter 47
paragraphs: About the strange way Don Quixote of La Mancha was carried off under enchantment, with other remarkable incidents

When Don Quixote found himself caged and hoisted onto the cart like this, he said, "I have read many serious histories of knights-errant, but never yet have I read, seen, or heard of their carrying off enchanted knights-errant in this fashion, or at the slow pace these lazy, sluggish beasts promise. They always take them through the air with marvellous swiftness, wrapped in a thick dark cloud, or on a chariot of fire, or perhaps on some hippogriff or other beast of the kind. But to carry me off like this on an ox-cart — by God, it puzzles me. Perhaps the chivalry and enchantments of our day take a different course from those of times gone by. And it may be too that, as I am a new knight in the world, the first to revive the long-forgotten calling of knight-adventurers, they have newly invented other kinds of enchantments and other ways of carrying off the enchanted. What do you make of it, Sancho my son?"

"I don't know what to make of it," Sancho answered, "not being as well read as your worship in chivalric writings; but for all that I'll venture to say and swear that these apparitions hovering around us are not quite Catholic."

"Catholic!" said Don Quixote. "Good heavens, how can they be Catholic when they're all devils in fantastic shapes, come here to do this and reduce me to this state? And if you want proof, touch them, feel them, and you'll find they have only bodies of air, no substance except in appearance."

"By God, master," Sancho returned, "I've already touched them, and that devil bustling about over there has firm flesh, and a property quite different from what I've heard tell of devils. By all accounts they all smell of brimstone and other bad smells; but this one smells of amber half a league off." Sancho was speaking of Don Fernando, who, as a gentleman of his rank, was very likely perfumed as Sancho said.

"Don't marvel at that, Sancho my friend," said Don Quixote. "Let me tell you: devils are cunning, and even if they carry scents about them, they themselves have no smell, because they're spirits; or if they do have a smell, it can't be of anything sweet but of something foul and stinking. The reason is that, since they carry hell with them wherever they go and can get no relief from their torments, and since a sweet smell gives pleasure and enjoyment, it's impossible they should smell sweet. If this devil you speak of seems to you to smell of amber, either you're deceiving yourself, or he's trying to deceive you by making you fancy he's not a devil."

Such was the conversation between master and man. Don Fernando and Cardenio, worried that Sancho might fully see through their scheme — towards which he had already gone some way — resolved to hasten their departure. Calling the landlord aside, they ordered him to saddle Rocinante and put the pack-saddle on Sancho's ass, which he did with great speed. Meanwhile the curate had arranged with the officers that they should accompany them as far as his village, he paying them so much a day. Cardenio hung the buckler on one side of the bow of Rocinante's saddle and the basin on the other, and by signs ordered Sancho to mount his ass and take Rocinante's bridle. At each side of the cart he placed two officers with their muskets. But before the cart was set in motion, the landlady, her daughter, and Maritornes came out to bid Don Quixote farewell, pretending to weep with grief at his misfortune. To them Don Quixote said:

"Weep not, good ladies, for all these mishaps are the lot of those who follow the profession I profess. If such setbacks did not befall me I should not count myself a famous knight-errant, for such things never happen to knights of little renown and fame, because no one in the world gives them a thought. They happen to valiant knights, for these are envied for their virtue and valour by many princes and other knights, who plot the destruction of the worthy by base means. Nevertheless, virtue is in itself so mighty that, in spite of all the magic that Zoroaster, its first inventor, knew, she will come victorious out of every trial and shed her light upon the earth as the sun does upon the heavens. Forgive me, fair ladies, if through inadvertence I have in any way offended you, for intentionally and knowingly I have never offended anyone. Pray to God that He deliver me from this captivity to which some malevolent enchanter has consigned me; and should I find myself freed, the favours you have shown me in this castle shall be held in memory by me, that I may acknowledge, recognise, and repay them as they deserve."

While this was passing between the ladies of the castle and Don Quixote, the curate and the barber said goodbye to Don Fernando and his companions, to the captain, his brother, and the ladies — now all made happy — and especially to Dorothea and Luscinda. They all embraced and promised to let one another know how things went, and Don Fernando told the curate where to write to him to report what became of Don Quixote, assuring him that nothing could give him more pleasure than to hear of it; he himself, in turn, would send word of everything he thought the curate would like to know — his marriage, Zoraida's baptism, Don Luis's situation, and Luscinda's return home. The curate promised to comply with the request carefully, and they embraced once more and renewed their promises.

The landlord went up to the curate and handed him some papers, saying he had found them in the lining of the valise in which the novel of "The Ill-advised Curiosity" had been found, and that the curate could take them all since their owner had not returned; he could not read them himself. The curate thanked him, and on opening them saw at the beginning of the manuscript the words "Novel of Rinconete and Cortadillo," by which he could tell it was a novel. Since "The Ill-advised Curiosity" had been good, he concluded this one would be too, since they were probably by the same author; so he kept it, intending to read it when he had the chance. He then mounted up, and his friend the barber did the same — both masked, so Don Quixote wouldn't recognise them — and they set out following behind the cart. The order of march was this: first went the cart with the owner leading it; on each side marched the officers of the Brotherhood, as already mentioned, with their muskets; then came Sancho Panza on his ass, leading Rocinante by the bridle; and bringing up the rear were the curate and the barber on their stout mules, faces covered as said, with a grave and serious bearing, measuring their pace to the slow steps of the oxen. Don Quixote sat in the cage with his hands tied and his feet stretched out, leaning against the bars, as silent and patient as a stone statue rather than a man of flesh. Going slowly and silently they made perhaps two leagues until they reached a valley which the carter thought a good place to rest and feed his oxen. He said as much to the curate, but the barber thought they should push on a little farther, because on the other side of a hill that appeared close by he knew of a valley with more and better grass. His advice was taken, and they continued on.

Just then the curate, glancing back, saw six or seven mounted men coming up behind, well outfitted and equipped, who soon caught up with them, for they were travelling not at the sluggish pace of oxen but like men riding canons' mules, in a hurry to take their noontide rest as soon as possible at the inn that was in sight not a league off. The quick travellers met up with the slow ones, and courteous greetings were exchanged. One of the newcomers, who was in fact a canon of Toledo and master of the others with him, observed the orderly procession — the cart, the officers, Sancho, Rocinante, the curate and the barber, and above all Don Quixote caged and confined — and could not help asking what was meant by carrying the man in that fashion, though, from the officers' badges, he already concluded he must be some desperate highwayman or other criminal whose punishment fell within the Holy Brotherhood's jurisdiction. One of the officers to whom he put the question replied, "Let the gentleman himself tell you the meaning of his going this way, señor, because we don't know."

Don Quixote overheard the conversation and said, "Perhaps, gentlemen, you are versed and learned in matters of errant chivalry? If so, I'll tell you my misfortunes; if not, there's no point in my troubling myself to relate them." But here the curate and the barber, seeing the travellers were in conversation with Don Quixote, came forward, ready to answer in such a way as to keep their scheme from being discovered.

Replying to Don Quixote, the canon said, "To tell the truth, brother, I know more about books of chivalry than I do about Villalpando's elements of logic; so if that's all, you may safely tell me whatever you please."

"In God's name, then, señor," replied Don Quixote, "if that's so, I'll have you know that I am held enchanted in this cage by the envy and treachery of wicked enchanters, since virtue is more persecuted by the wicked than loved by the good. I am a knight-errant — and not one of those whose names Fame never thought of immortalising, but of those who, in defiance and despite of envy itself, and all the magicians that Persia, or Brahmans that India, or Gymnosophists that Ethiopia ever produced, will set their names in the temple of immortality, to serve as examples and patterns for ages to come, that knights-errant may see the footsteps in which they must tread to reach the summit and crowning point of honour in arms."

"What Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha says," observed the curate, "is the truth. He goes enchanted in this cart, not for any fault or sin of his, but because of the malice of those to whom virtue is odious and valour hateful. This, señor, is the Knight of the Rueful Countenance — if you've ever heard him named — whose valiant achievements and mighty deeds shall be written on lasting brass and imperishable marble, despite all the efforts of envy to obscure them and malice to hide them."

When the canon heard both the prisoner and the man who was at liberty speaking in this way, he was ready to cross himself in astonishment, and could not make out what was happening; all his attendants were in the same state of amazement.

At this point Sancho Panza, who had drawn near to hear the conversation, said, to make matters plain, "Well, sirs, you can like it or not, but the fact is, my master Don Quixote is just about as enchanted as my mother. He's in his full senses; he eats and he drinks and he answers nature's calls like other men, and as he did yesterday before they caged him. If that's the case, what do they mean by trying to make me believe he's enchanted? I've heard many a one say that enchanted people don't eat, sleep, or talk — and my master, if you don't stop him, will talk more than thirty lawyers." Then turning to the curate he exclaimed, "Ah, señor curate, señor curate! Do you think I don't know you? Do you think I can't guess what these new enchantments are about? Well, I can tell you I do know you, no matter how covered your face is, and I'm on to you, however much you hide your tricks. In the end, where envy reigns, virtue can't live, and where there's stinginess there can be no generosity. Curse the devil! If it hadn't been for your worship, my master would have been married to Princess Micomicona by now, and I'd be a count at least — for no less was to be expected, as much from the goodness of my master, him of the Rueful Countenance, as from the greatness of my services. But I see now how true it is what they say in these parts, that the wheel of fortune turns faster than a mill-wheel, and those who were up yesterday are down today. I'm sorry for my wife and children; when they could reasonably have hoped to see their father come back a governor or viceroy of some island or kingdom, they'll see him come home a stable-hand. I'm saying all this, señor curate, only to urge your paternity to take to your conscience this ill-treatment of my master, and to be careful that God doesn't call you to account in the next life for making him a prisoner this way, and charge against you all the rescues and good deeds my lord Don Quixote leaves undone while he's shut up."

"Trim those wicks!" exclaimed the barber at this. "So you're of the same fraternity as your master, are you, Sancho? By God, I'm starting to see you'll have to keep him company in the cage and be enchanted like him for having caught some of his humour and chivalry. It was an evil hour you let yourself be got with child by his promises, and that island you long for so much wormed its way into your head."

"I'm not with child by anyone," Sancho returned, "nor am I a man to let himself be got with child, not by the King himself. I may be poor, but I'm an old Christian, and I owe nothing to nobody; and if I long for an island, other people long for worse. Each of us is the son of his own works; and being a man I may come to be pope, never mind governor of an island — especially as my master may win so many that he won't know whom to give them to. Mind how you talk, master barber; for shaving isn't everything, and there's some difference between one Peter and another. I say this because we all know one another, and it won't do to throw false dice with me; and as for my master's enchantment, God knows the truth — leave it alone; it only gets worse when stirred."

The barber didn't bother answering Sancho, in case his plain speaking gave away what he and the curate were trying so hard to conceal. With the same worry in mind the curate had asked the canon to ride on a little ahead so he could tell him the mystery of the man in the cage, along with other things that would entertain him. The canon agreed, and going on ahead with his servants, listened attentively to the account the curate gave him of Don Quixote's character, life, madness, and ways — describing briefly the beginning and origin of his craze, telling the whole story of his adventures up to his being confined in the cage, and outlining their plan to take him home to see if any cure might be found for his madness. The canon and his servants were astonished anew at Don Quixote's strange story, and when it was finished he said, "To tell the truth, señor curate, for my part I consider what they call books of chivalry to be harmful to the State. Though, led by idle and false taste, I've read the beginnings of almost all that have been printed, I could never manage to finish a single one, because they all seem more or less the same thing — one has nothing more in it than another. And in my opinion this sort of writing and composition is of the same species as the fables they call Milesian: nonsensical tales aimed solely at amusement and not instruction, the exact opposite of the apologue fables which both amuse and instruct. And even if amusement be the chief object of such books, I don't see how they can succeed when they're so full of monstrous nonsense. The enjoyment the mind feels must come from the beauty and harmony it perceives in what the eye or the imagination puts before it, and nothing with ugliness or disproportion about it can give pleasure. What beauty, then, or what proportion of the parts to the whole or of the whole to the parts, can there be in a book or fable in which a lad of sixteen cuts down a giant tall as a tower and makes two halves of him as if he were an almond cake? Or when they want to give us a picture of a battle, after telling us there are a million combatants on the enemy's side, the hero of the book is set against them, and we are obliged to believe, whether we like it or not, that this knight wins the victory by the single might of his strong arm. And then, what shall we say of how easily a queen or empress by birth will throw herself into the arms of some unknown wandering knight? What mind, unless wholly barbarous and uncultivated, can take pleasure in reading how a great tower full of knights sails over the sea like a ship with a fair wind, tonight in Lombardy and tomorrow morning in the land of Prester John of the Indies, or some other land Ptolemy never described nor Marco Polo saw? And if I'm told that the authors of such books write them as fiction, and so are not obliged to worry about niceties of truth, my reply is that fiction is better the more it resembles truth, and gives the more pleasure the more probability and possibility there is about it. Plots in fiction must be wedded to the understanding of the reader, and constructed in such a way that, reconciling impossibilities, smoothing over difficulties, keeping the mind alert, they may surprise, interest, divert, and entertain, so that wonder and delight may keep pace one with the other. All of this will fail in any writer who avoids verisimilitude and truth to nature, in which the perfection of writing lies. I've never yet seen a book of chivalry that puts together a coherent plot complete in all its parts, so that the middle agrees with the beginning and the end with the beginning and middle; on the contrary, they're constructed with such a tangle of limbs that it seems as if the authors were trying to produce a chimera or monster rather than a well-proportioned figure. And besides all this they are harsh in style, incredible in their feats, lascivious in their love-affairs, uncouth in their courtly speeches, prolix in their battles, silly in their arguments, absurd in their travels, and in short wanting in everything resembling intelligent art — for which reason they deserve to be banished from the Christian commonwealth as a worthless breed."

The curate listened attentively and felt the man was of sound understanding, and that there was good sense in what he said. So he told him that, being of the same opinion himself and bearing a grudge against books of chivalry, he had burned all of Don Quixote's — which were many — and gave him an account of the scrutiny he had made of them, of those he had condemned to the flames and those he had spared, all of which amused the canon a good deal. The canon added that though he had said so much in condemnation of these books, he did find one good thing in them: they afforded a gifted intellect a chance to display itself, since they offered a wide and spacious field over which the pen might range freely — describing shipwrecks, tempests, combats, battles, portraying a valiant captain with all the qualifications required to be one, showing him shrewd in foreseeing the enemy's wiles, eloquent in encouraging or restraining his soldiers, mature in counsel, swift in resolve, as bold in biding his time as in pressing the attack; now picturing some sad, tragic incident, now some joyful and unexpected event; here a beautiful lady, virtuous, wise, and modest; there a Christian knight, brave and gentle; here a lawless, barbarous braggart; there a courteous prince, gallant and gracious; setting forth the devotion and loyalty of vassals, the greatness and generosity of nobles. "Or again," he said, "the author may show himself as an astronomer, or a skilled cosmographer, or musician, or one versed in affairs of state, and at times he'll have the chance to appear as a magician if he likes. He can set forth the craftiness of Ulysses, the piety of Æneas, the valour of Achilles, the misfortunes of Hector, the treachery of Sinon, the friendship of Euryalus, the generosity of Alexander, the boldness of Cæsar, the clemency and truth of Trajan, the fidelity of Zopyrus, the wisdom of Cato — and in short all the qualities that go to make an illustrious man perfect, now uniting them in a single character, now distributing them among many; and if this be done with charm of style and ingenious invention, aiming at truth as much as possible, he will surely weave a web of bright and varied threads which, when finished, will display such perfection and beauty that it will attain the worthiest object any writing can seek — to give instruction and pleasure combined; for the unrestricted range of these books lets the author show his powers in the epic, lyric, tragic, or comic vein, and all the moods the sweet and winning arts of poetry and oratory are capable of, since the epic may be written in prose just as well as in verse."

title: Part 1, Chapter 48
paragraphs: In which the canon continues on the subject of books of chivalry, with other matters worthy of his wit

"You are quite right, señor canon," said the curate; "and for that reason those who have so far written books of this sort deserve all the more censure for writing without paying any attention to good taste or the rules of art — by which they might have guided themselves and become as famous in prose as the two princes of Greek and Latin poetry are in verse."

"For my part," said the canon, "I was once tempted to write a book of chivalry in which all the points I've mentioned were to be observed; and if I must confess the truth, I have more than a hundred pages written. To test whether it lived up to my own opinion of it, I showed them to people who were fond of this kind of reading — to learned and intelligent men as well as to ignorant people who care for nothing but the pleasure of listening to nonsense — and from all of them I got flattering approval. Nevertheless I went no farther with it, both because it seemed to me an occupation inconsistent with my profession and because I saw that the fools are more numerous than the wise; and though it's better to be praised by the wise few than applauded by the foolish many, I have no wish to submit myself to the stupid judgment of the silly public, to whom the reading of such books falls for the most part.

"But what most made me hold my hand and even give up the idea of finishing it was an argument I put to myself drawn from the plays performed nowadays. It went like this: if those now in vogue — both the pure inventions and those founded on history — are, all or most of them, downright nonsense and things with neither head nor tail; and yet the public listens to them with delight and proclaims them perfect when they're far from it; and if the authors who write them and the players who act them say that this is what they must be, because the public wants this and nothing else; and that those who follow the rules and work out a plot according to the laws of art will only find some half-dozen intelligent people to understand them, while everyone else remains blind to the merit of their composition; and that for themselves it's better to get bread from the many than praise from the few — well then, my book will fare the same way, after I have scorched my eyebrows trying to observe the principles I've mentioned, and I shall be 'the tailor of the corner.' Though I've sometimes tried to convince actors they're mistaken in the opinion they've adopted, and that they would draw bigger audiences and earn more credit by producing plays that observe the rules of art rather than absurd ones, they are so thoroughly wedded to their own view that no argument or evidence can wean them from it.

"I remember saying one day to one of these obstinate fellows, 'Tell me, don't you remember that a few years ago there were three tragedies acted in Spain, written by a famous poet of these kingdoms, which were such that they filled all who heard them with admiration, delight, and interest — the ignorant as well as the wise, the masses as well as the higher orders — and brought in more money to the performers, these three alone, than thirty of the best produced since?'
"'No doubt,' replied the actor in question, 'you mean the "Isabella," the "Phyllis," and the "Alexandra."'

"'Those are the ones I mean,' I said; 'and see whether they didn't observe the principles of art, and whether, by observing them, they failed to show their superiority and please everyone. So the fault doesn't lie with the public that insists on nonsense, but with those who don't know how to produce anything else. "The Ingratitude Revenged" was not nonsense, nor was there any in "The Numantia," nor any to be found in "The Merchant Lover," nor yet in "The Friendly Fair Foe," nor in some others that have been written by certain gifted poets — to their own fame and renown and to the profit of those who brought them out.' I added a few more remarks to these, which I think left him rather dumbfounded but not so satisfied or convinced that I could disabuse him of his error."

"You've touched on a subject, señor canon," observed the curate, "that has awoken an old grievance of mine against the plays now in vogue — as strong as the one I bear against the books of chivalry. The drama, according to Tully, should be the mirror of human life, the model of manners, and the image of the truth; but those put on these days are mirrors of nonsense, models of folly, and images of lewdness. For what greater nonsense can there be on this subject than for an infant to appear in swaddling clothes in the first scene of the first act, and in the second a grown-up bearded man? Or what greater absurdity than putting before us an old man as a swashbuckler, a young man as a coward, a lackey using fine language, a page giving sage advice, a king moonlighting as a porter, or a princess as a kitchen-maid? And what shall I say of their concern for the time in which the action they represent could conceivably take place — except that I've seen a play where the first act began in Europe, the second in Asia, the third ended in Africa, and no doubt, had it had four acts, the fourth would have ended in America, so it would have been laid in all four quarters of the globe? And if truth to life is the main thing the drama should keep in view, how can any average understanding be satisfied when the action is supposed to pass in the time of King Pepin or Charlemagne, and the principal character in it is the Emperor Heraclius, who entered Jerusalem with the cross and won the Holy Sepulchre, like Godfrey of Bouillon — there being countless years between the two? Or, if the play is based on fiction, historical facts are introduced, or bits of what happened to different people at different times are mixed up with it, all with no semblance of probability but with obvious errors that from every point of view are inexcusable? And the worst of it is, there are ignorant people who say this is perfection and that anything beyond it is mere affectation. And then if we turn to sacred dramas — what miracles they invent in them! What apocryphal, ill-devised incidents, attributing to one saint the miracles of another! Even in secular plays they venture to introduce miracles without any reason or purpose except that they think some such miracle, or transformation as they call it, will go down well with the dim-witted and draw them to the play. All this tends to the prejudice of the truth and the corruption of history — indeed, to the disgrace of Spanish wit, for foreigners who scrupulously observe the laws of the drama look on us as barbarous and ignorant when they see the absurdity and nonsense of the plays we produce. Nor is it a sufficient excuse to say that the chief object well-ordered governments have in view when they permit public plays is to entertain the people with some harmless amusement now and then and keep them clear of the evil humours that idleness tends to breed, and that, as this may be achieved by any sort of play, good or bad, there's no need to lay down laws or bind those who write or act them to make them as they ought to be — since, as I say, the object sought may be achieved by any sort. To which I'd reply that the same end would be, beyond all comparison, better attained by good plays than by those that aren't, for after listening to an artistic and well-constructed play the hearer will come away enlivened by the jokes, instructed by the serious parts, full of admiration at the incidents, his wits sharpened by the arguments, warned by the deceptions, all the wiser for the examples, inflamed against vice, and in love with virtue; for in all these ways a good play will stir the mind of any hearer, however boorish or dull. And of all impossibilities the greatest is that a play endowed with all these qualities should not entertain, satisfy, and please much more than one wanting in them — like most of those commonly acted now. Nor are the poets who write them to be blamed; for some of them are perfectly aware of their faults and know what they should do, but since plays have become a saleable commodity, they say — and truly — that actors won't buy them unless they're after this fashion, so the poet tries to adapt to the requirements of the actor who's going to pay him. The proof can be seen in the countless plays a most fertile wit of these kingdoms has written, with such brilliance, such grace and gaiety, such polished versification, such choice language, such profound reflections — in a word, so rich in eloquence and elevation of style — that he has filled the world with his fame; and yet, because of his desire to suit the actors' taste, they haven't all, as some of them have, come as near perfection as they ought. Others write plays so carelessly that, after they've been acted, the actors have to flee and go into hiding for fear of being punished (as they often have been) for having acted something offensive to some king or other, or insulting to some noble family. All these evils, and many more I'm passing over, would be removed if at the capital there were some intelligent and sensible person to examine all plays before they were acted — not only those produced in the capital itself, but all that were meant to be acted in Spain — without whose approval, seal, and signature no local magistracy should allow any play to be performed. In that case actors would take care to send their plays to the capital, and could act them in safety; and those who write them would be more careful and take more pains with their work, knowing they would have to submit it to the strict examination of someone who understood the matter. So good plays would be produced, and the objects they aim at happily attained: the amusement of the people, the credit of Spanish wit, the interest and safety of the actors, and the saving of trouble in inflicting punishment on them. And if the same or some other person were authorised to examine the newly written books of chivalry, no doubt some would appear with all the perfections you've described, enriching our language with the gracious and precious treasure of eloquence, and driving the old books into obscurity before the light of the new ones, which would come out for the harmless entertainment not only of the idle but of the very busiest; for the bow cannot always be bent, nor can weak human nature exist without some lawful amusement."

The canon and the curate had gone this far with their conversation when the barber came up and joined them, saying to the curate, "This is the spot, señor licentiate, I said was a good one for fresh and plentiful pasture for the oxen while we take our noontide rest."

"So it seems," the curate replied, and he told the canon what he was planning to do. The canon, too, decided to halt with them, drawn by the look of the fair valley before them; and to enjoy it as well as the curate's conversation — for he had taken a liking to him — and to learn more about Don Quixote's doings, he directed some of his servants to ride on to the inn, which was not far off, and fetch whatever food there might be for the whole party, since he intended to rest for the afternoon where they were. One of his servants replied that the sumpter mule, which by now should have reached the inn, was carrying enough provisions to make it unnecessary to get anything from the inn except barley.
"In that case," said the canon, "take all the beasts there and bring the sumpter mule back."

While this was going on, Sancho, seeing he could speak to his master without the curate and the barber, of whom he was suspicious, being present all the time, came up to the cage in which Don Quixote sat and said, "Señor, to ease my conscience I want to tell you the truth about your enchantment, which is that these two men with their faces covered are the curate of our village and the barber. I suspect they've hit on this plan of carrying you off out of pure envy, because your worship surpasses them in doing famous deeds. And if that's the truth, it follows you are not enchanted but hoodwinked and made a fool of. And to prove this I want to ask you one thing; if you answer me as I believe you will, you'll be able to put your finger on the trick and see that you're not enchanted but out of your wits."

"Ask whatever you like, Sancho my son," Don Quixote returned, "and I will satisfy you and answer all you ask. As for what you say — that those accompanying us yonder are the curate and the barber, our neighbours and acquaintances — it is very possible they may seem to be those very people; but that they really and truly are so, don't believe it on any account. What you must believe and think is that if they look like them, as you say, it must be that those who have enchanted me have taken this shape and likeness; for enchanters can easily take any form they choose, and they may have taken those of our friends in order to make you think as you do, and lead you into a labyrinth of fancies from which you would not escape even if you had the thread of Theseus. They may also have done it to make me uncertain in my mind, unable to guess where this evil comes from. For if on the one hand you tell me the barber and curate of our village are here with us, and on the other I find myself shut up in a cage, knowing in my heart that no power on earth, short of the supernatural, could have shut me in, what would you have me say or think, except that my enchantment is of a kind that surpasses anything I have ever read of in all the histories that deal with enchanted knights-errant? So you may set your mind at rest about the idea that they are what you say, for they are as much that as I am a Turk. But as for what you want to ask me — ask away, and I'll answer, even if you have to keep asking questions from now till tomorrow morning."

"Our Lady help me!" said Sancho, raising his voice. "Is it possible your worship is so thick of skull and so short of brains that you can't see what I say is the simple truth, and that malice has more to do with your imprisonment and misfortune than enchantment? Since that's how things are, I'll prove plainly to you that you are not enchanted. Now tell me, so God may deliver you from this affliction, and so you may find yourself when you least expect it in the arms of my lady Dulcinea —"
"Stop conjuring me," said Don Quixote, "and ask what you want to know; I've already told you I'll answer as precisely as possible."

"That's what I want," said Sancho, "and what I'd like to know, and have you tell me, without adding or leaving anything out, but telling the whole truth as one expects it to be told, and as it is told, by all who profess arms, as your worship does, under the title of knights-errant —"
"I tell you I won't lie in any particular," said Don Quixote; "finish your question, for in truth you wear me out with all these vows, demands, and precautions, Sancho."

"Well, I rely on my master's goodness and truthfulness," said Sancho; "and so, because it bears on what we're talking about, I would ask, speaking with all reverence, whether since your worship has been shut up and, as you think, enchanted in this cage, you've felt any desire or inclination to go anywhere, as the saying is?"
"I don't understand 'going anywhere,'" said Don Quixote; "explain yourself more clearly, Sancho, if you want me to give a straight answer."

"Is it possible," said Sancho, "that your worship doesn't understand 'going anywhere'? Why, schoolboys know that from the time they were babies. Well then, I mean — have you had any desire to do what cannot be avoided?"
"Ah, now I understand you, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "Yes, often, and right at this minute. Get me out of this fix, or things won't end well."

title: Part 1, Chapter 49
paragraphs: Which treats of the shrewd conversation that Sancho Panza held with his master Don Quixote

"Aha, I've caught you," said Sancho. "This is what in my heart and soul I was longing to know. Come on now, señor, can you deny what people commonly say around here when somebody is out of sorts: 'I don't know what ails so-and-so, that he won't eat, or drink, or sleep, or give a proper answer to any question; you'd think he was enchanted'? From which it follows that those who don't eat, or drink, or sleep, or do any of the natural acts I'm talking about — those people are enchanted; but not those who have the desire your worship has, and drink when drink is given them, and eat when there's anything to eat, and answer every question put to them."

"What you say is true, Sancho," replied Don Quixote, "but I've already told you there are many kinds of enchantments; and it may be that in the course of time they've changed from one to another, and that now it may be the way with enchanted people to do all that I do, though they didn't do so before. So it's pointless to argue or draw inferences against the usage of the time. I know and feel that I am enchanted, and that is enough to ease my conscience; for it would weigh on me heavily if I thought I was not enchanted, and that in a faint-hearted and cowardly way I was letting myself lie in this cage, defrauding multitudes of the help I might give to those in need and distress, who at this very moment may be in dire want of my aid and protection."

"Still for all that," Sancho replied, "I say that, for your greater and fuller satisfaction, it would be well if your worship were to try to get out of this prison — and I promise to do all I can to help, and even to take you out of it — and see if you could once more mount your good Rocinante, who seems enchanted too, he's so melancholy and dejected. Then we might try our luck looking for adventures again; and if we have no luck there will be time enough to go back to the cage; in which, on the faith of a good and loyal squire, I promise to shut myself up alongside your worship, if you're so unfortunate, or I so stupid, as not to manage to carry out my plan."

"I'm content to do as you say, brother Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and when you see an opportunity for my release I'll obey you absolutely; but you'll see, Sancho, how mistaken you are in your view of my misfortune."

The knight-errant and the wayward squire kept up their conversation till they reached the place where the curate, the canon, and the barber, who had already dismounted, were waiting for them. The carter at once unyoked the oxen and left them to roam freely about the pleasant green spot, the freshness of which seemed to invite — not enchanted people like Don Quixote, but wide-awake, sensible folk like his squire, who begged the curate to allow his master to leave the cage for a little while; otherwise the prison might not be as clean as the dignity of a gentleman like his master required. The curate understood, and said he would happily comply, only that he feared his master, finding himself at liberty, would revert to his old ways and bolt off where no one could find him again.
"I'll answer for his not running away," said Sancho.
"And I as well," said the canon, "especially if he gives me his word as a knight not to leave us without our consent."

Don Quixote, who was listening to all this, said, "I give it; what's more, one who is enchanted as I am cannot do as he likes with himself; for the one who enchanted him could keep him from moving from one place for three ages, and if he tried to escape would bring him back flying." That being so, they might as well release him, particularly as it would be to everyone's advantage; for, if they didn't let him out, he warned that he wouldn't be able to avoid offending their nostrils unless they kept their distance.

The canon took his hand — even though they were still tied together — and on his word and promise they untied him, and he rejoiced beyond measure to find himself out of the cage. The first thing he did was stretch all over, then he went over to where Rocinante was standing, and giving him a couple of slaps on the haunches said, "I still trust in God and in his blessed mother, O flower and mirror of steeds, that we shall soon see ourselves, both of us, as we wish to be — you with your master on your back, and I mounted on you, following the calling for which God sent me into the world." Saying this, and accompanied by Sancho, he withdrew to a private spot, from which he came back much relieved and more eager than ever to put his squire's plan into action.

The canon studied him, marvelling at the extraordinary nature of his madness, and that in all his remarks and replies he showed such excellent sense, and only lost his stirrups, as has already been noted, when the subject of chivalry was broached. So, moved by compassion, he said to him, as they all sat on the green grass waiting for the provisions to arrive:

"Is it possible, my good sir, that the dull and idle reading of books of chivalry can have had such an effect on your worship as to upset your reason, so that you fancy yourself enchanted and the like — all as far from the truth as falsehood itself? How can any human understanding persuade itself that there ever was all that infinity of Amadises in the world, all that multitude of famous knights, all those emperors of Trebizond, all those Felixmartes of Hircania, all those palfreys and damsels-errant, and serpents, and monsters, and giants, and marvellous adventures, and enchantments of every kind, and battles, and prodigious encounters, splendid costumes, love-sick princesses, squires made counts, droll dwarfs, love letters, billing and cooing, swashbuckling women — in a word, all the nonsense the books of chivalry contain? For myself, I can only say that when I read them, as long as I don't stop to think they're all lies and trifles, they give me a certain amount of pleasure; but when I come to consider what they really are, I fling the very best of them at the wall, and would fling it into the fire if there were one at hand, as richly deserving such punishment — being cheats and impostors beyond the range of ordinary toleration, founders of new sects and modes of life, teachers who lead the ignorant public to believe and accept as truth all the folly they contain. And their audacity is such, they even dare to unsettle the wits of gentlemen of birth and intelligence, as is plainly shown by how they have served your worship, bringing you to such a pass that you have to be shut up in a cage and carried on an ox-cart like a lion or a tiger that's hauled around to make money by showing it off. Come, Señor Don Quixote, have some compassion for yourself, return to the bosom of common sense, and put to use the liberal share of it that heaven has been pleased to bestow upon you, employing your abundant gifts of mind in some other reading that may benefit your conscience and add to your honour. And if, still led away by your natural bent, you wish to read books of exploits and chivalry, read the Book of Judges in Holy Scripture, for there you'll find grand reality, and deeds as true as they are heroic. Lusitania had a Viriatus, Rome a Cæsar, Carthage a Hannibal, Greece an Alexander, Castile a Count Fernan Gonzalez, Valencia a Cid, Andalusia a Gonzalo Fernandez, Estremadura a Diego García de Paredes, Jerez a Garci Perez de Vargas, Toledo a Garcilaso, Seville a Don Manuel de Leon — to read of whose valiant deeds will entertain and instruct the loftiest minds and fill them with delight and wonder. Here, Señor Don Quixote, you'll find reading worthy of your sound understanding; from which you'll rise learned in history, in love with virtue, strengthened in goodness, improved in manners, brave without recklessness, prudent without cowardice — all to the honour of God, your own advantage, and the glory of La Mancha, where I am told your worship was born."
Don Quixote listened with the greatest attention to the canon's words, and when he found he had finished, after looking at him for some time, he replied:

"It appears to me, gentle sir, that your worship's argument is intended to persuade me that no knights-errant ever existed in the world, and that all the books of chivalry are false, lying, mischievous, and useless to the State, and that I have done wrong in reading them, worse in believing them, and worse still in imitating them when I undertook to follow the demanding calling of knight-errantry which they set out — for you deny that there were ever any Amadises of Gaul or of Greece, or any of the other knights of whom the books are full."

"It is exactly as you state it," said the canon. To which Don Quixote returned, "You also went on to say that books of this kind have done me a great deal of harm, in that they've upset my senses and got me shut up in a cage, and that it would be better for me to reform and change my reading, and read other, truer books which would afford more pleasure and instruction."
"Just so," said the canon.

"Well then," returned Don Quixote, "in my view it's you who are the one out of his wits and enchanted, since you have dared to utter such blasphemies against a thing so universally acknowledged and accepted as true that whoever denies it, as you do, deserves the same punishment you say you inflict on books that irritate you when you read them. For trying to persuade anyone that Amadis, and all the other knights-adventurers with whom the books are filled, never existed would be like trying to persuade him that the sun doesn't yield light, or ice cold, or earth nourishment. What wit in the world can persuade another that the story of Princess Floripes and Guy of Burgundy is not true, or that of Fierabras and the bridge of Mantible, which happened in the time of Charlemagne? By all that is good, it is as true as it is daylight now; and if it's a lie, then it must be a lie too that there was a Hector, or Achilles, or Trojan war, or Twelve Peers of France, or Arthur of England, who still lives changed into a raven and is endlessly looked for in his kingdom.
