One might just as well try to argue that the history of Guarino Mezquino, or the quest of the Holy Grail, is false; or that the loves of Tristram and Queen Yseult are made up, as well as those of Guinevere and Lancelot — when there are people who can almost remember having seen Dame Quintañona, who was the best cupbearer in Great Britain. And so true is this, that I recall a grandmother of mine on my father's side, whenever she saw any dame in a venerable hood, used to say to me, 'Grandson, that one looks like Dame Quintañona,' from which I conclude she must have known her, or at least seen some portrait of her. Then who can deny that the story of Pierres and the fair Magalona is true, when even to this day in the king's armoury you can see the pin with which the valiant Pierres steered the wooden horse he rode through the air, and it's a trifle bigger than the pole of a cart? Alongside the pin is Babieca's saddle, and at Roncesvalles there's Roland's horn, as large as a great beam; from which we may infer that there were Twelve Peers, and a Pierres, and a Cid, and other knights like them — of the kind people commonly call adventurers. Or perhaps I'll be told too that there was no such knight-errant as the valiant Lusitanian Juan de Merlo, who went to Burgundy and in the city of Arras fought with the famous lord of Charny, Mosen Pierres by name, and afterwards in the city of Basle with Mosen Enrique de Remesten, coming out of both encounters covered with fame and honour; or the adventures and challenges achieved and delivered, also in Burgundy, by the valiant Spaniards Pedro Barba and Gutierre Quixada (from whose family I come in the direct male line), when they vanquished the sons of the Count of San Polo. I shall be told too that Don Fernando de Guevara did not go in search of adventures to Germany, where he engaged in combat with Micer George, a knight of the house of the Duke of Austria. I shall be told that the jousts of Suero de Quiñones, him of the 'Paso,' and the enterprise of Mosen Luis de Falces against the Castilian knight Don Gonzalo de Guzman, were mere mockeries; as well as many other achievements of Christian knights of these and foreign realms, which are so authentic and true that, I repeat, anyone who denies them must be totally wanting in reason and good sense."
The canon was astonished to hear the medley of truth and fiction Don Quixote was producing, and to see how well acquainted he was with everything relating to his knight-errantry; so he said in reply:

"I cannot deny, Señor Don Quixote, that there is some truth in what you say, especially as regards the Spanish knights-errant. I'm willing to grant too that the Twelve Peers of France existed, but I'm not prepared to believe that they did all the things Archbishop Turpin relates of them. The truth of the matter is they were knights chosen by the kings of France, called 'Peers' because they were all equal in worth, rank, and prowess (or at least if they weren't they ought to have been); and it was a kind of religious order like those of Santiago and Calatrava today, in which it is taken for granted that those who take it on are valiant knights of distinction and good birth. Just as we say now 'a Knight of St. John,' or 'of Alcántara,' they used to say then 'a Knight of the Twelve Peers,' because twelve equals were chosen for that military order. That there was a Cid, as well as a Bernardo del Carpio, there can be no doubt; but that they did the deeds people say they did, I hold to be very doubtful. As for the other matter — the pin of Count Pierres you mention, and say is near Babieca's saddle in the Armoury — I confess my sin: I am either so stupid or so short-sighted that, though I've seen the saddle, I've never been able to spot the pin, despite its being as big as your worship says."
"For all that, it is there, no doubt about it," said Don Quixote; "and what's more, they say it is enclosed in a sheath of cowhide to keep it from rusting."

"All that may be," replied the canon; "but by the orders I have taken, I don't recall seeing it. However, granting that it's there, that's no reason why I'm obliged to believe the stories of all those Amadises and of the whole multitude of knights they tell us about; nor is it reasonable that a man like your worship, so worthy, with so many good qualities and endowed with such a sound understanding, should let himself be persuaded that the wild crazy things written in those absurd books of chivalry are really true."

title: Part 1, Chapter 50
paragraphs: About the shrewd dispute Don Quixote and the canon held, with other incidents

"A fine joke, that!" returned Don Quixote. "Books printed with the king's licence, and with the approval of those they've been submitted to, and read with universal delight, and praised by great and small, rich and poor, learned and ignorant, gentle and simple — in a word, by people of every sort, of whatever rank or condition — that these should be lies! And above all when they bear such an air of truth about them, telling us the father, mother, country, kindred, age, place, and the deeds, step by step and day by day, performed by such a knight or knights. Hush, sir, don't utter such blasphemy; trust me, I'm advising you now to act as a sensible man should — just read them, and you'll see the pleasure you'll derive. Come, tell me, can there be anything more delightful than to see, as it were, displayed before us a vast lake of bubbling pitch with a host of snakes and serpents and lizards, and all sorts of fierce and terrible creatures swimming about in it, while from the middle of the lake comes a plaintive voice saying: 'Knight, whoever you are who behold this dread lake, if you would win the prize hidden beneath these dusky waves, prove the valour of your stout heart and cast yourself into the midst of its dark burning waters, else you shall not be worthy to see the mighty wonders contained in the seven castles of the seven Fays that lie beneath this black expanse'? And then the knight, almost before the awful voice has finished, without stopping to think, without pausing to reflect on the danger he is exposing himself to, without even relieving himself of the weight of his massive armour, commending himself to God and to his lady, plunges into the middle of the boiling lake; and when he least expects it, or knows what his fate is to be, he finds himself among flowery meadows with which the Elysian Fields cannot compare.

"The sky there seems more transparent, and the sun shines with a strange brilliance. A delightful grove of green leafy trees presents itself to the eye and charms the sight with its greenness, while the ear is soothed by the sweet untutored melody of the countless gay-plumaged birds flitting to and fro among the interlacing branches. Here he sees a brook whose clear waters, like liquid crystal, ripple over fine sands and white pebbles that look like sifted gold and the purest pearls. Over there he sees a cunningly wrought fountain of many-coloured jasper and polished marble; here another in rustic style, where the little mussel-shells and the spiral white and yellow houses of the snail, arranged in studied disorder, mingled with fragments of glittering crystal and mock emeralds, make up a work of varied appearance in which art, imitating nature, seems to have outdone it.

"Suddenly there is presented to his sight a strong castle or gorgeous palace with walls of solid gold, turrets of diamond, and gates of jacinth; in short, so marvellous in construction that, though the materials it is built of are nothing less than diamonds, carbuncles, rubies, pearls, gold, and emeralds, the workmanship is still more rare. And after seeing all this, what can be more charming than to see how a bevy of damsels come forth from the gate of the castle in gay and gorgeous attire, such that, were I to set myself now to depict it as the histories describe it to us, I would never be done? Then how she who appears to be first among them takes the bold knight who plunged into the boiling lake by the hand, and without saying a word leads him into the rich palace or castle, and strips him as naked as when his mother bore him, and bathes him in lukewarm water, and anoints him all over with sweet-smelling ointments, and clothes him in a shirt of the softest sendal, all scented and perfumed, while another damsel comes and throws over his shoulders a mantle said to be worth at the very least a city, and more besides. How charming, then, when they tell us how, after all this, they lead him to another chamber where he finds the tables set out in such style that he is filled with amazement and wonder; to see how they pour out water for his hands distilled from amber and sweet-scented flowers; how they seat him on an ivory chair; to see how the damsels wait on him all in profound silence; how they bring him such a variety of delicacies, so temptingly prepared, that the appetite is at a loss which to choose; to hear the music that plays while he is at table, by whom or whence produced he knows not. And then when the meal is over and the tables removed, for the knight to recline in his chair, picking his teeth perhaps as usual — and a damsel, much lovelier than any of the others, to enter unexpectedly through the chamber door and seat herself by his side, and begin to tell him what the castle is, and how she is held enchanted there, and other things that amaze the knight and astonish the readers who follow his story.

"But I won't go on at greater length about this, as it can be gathered from it that whatever part of whatever history of a knight-errant one reads, it will fill the reader, whoever he is, with delight and wonder. So take my advice, sir, and, as I said before, read these books and you'll see how they will banish any melancholy you may feel and raise your spirits if they're depressed. For myself I can say that since I have been a knight-errant I have become valiant, polite, generous, well-bred, magnanimous, courteous, dauntless, gentle, patient, and have learned to endure hardships, imprisonments, and enchantments. And though it's only a short time since I have seen myself shut up in a cage like a madman, I hope by the might of my arm — if heaven aids me and fortune doesn't thwart me — to see myself king of some kingdom where I may show the gratitude and generosity that dwell in my heart. For by my faith, señor, the poor man is incapable of showing the virtue of generosity to anyone, though he may possess it in the highest degree; and gratitude that consists only in disposition is a dead thing, just as faith without works is dead. For this reason I should be glad if fortune would soon offer me some opportunity to make myself an emperor, so as to show my heart in doing good to my friends, particularly to this poor Sancho Panza, my squire, who is the best fellow in the world; and I'd gladly give him a county I have promised him this long while, only that I'm afraid he doesn't have the capacity to govern his realm."

Sancho caught the last of his master's words and said, "Strive hard, Señor Don Quixote, to give me that county so often promised by you and so long looked for by me; I promise you there'll be no lack of capacity in me to govern it. And even if there is, I've heard say there are men in the world who farm their estates, paying so much a year, and themselves take charge of the government, while the lord, with his legs stretched out, enjoys the revenue they pay him without bothering himself about anything else. That's what I'll do — not stand haggling over trifles, but wash my hands at once of the whole business, and enjoy my rents like a duke, and let things take their course."

"That, brother Sancho," said the canon, "only holds good as far as the enjoyment of the revenue goes; but the lord of the seigniory must attend to the administration of justice, and there capacity and sound judgment come in — and above all a firm determination to find out the truth; for if this is wanting at the beginning, the middle and end will always go wrong; and God commonly aids the honest intentions of the simple as he frustrates the evil designs of the crafty."

"I don't understand those philosophies," returned Sancho Panza. "All I know is I wish I had the county as soon as I'd know how to govern it; for I have as much soul as another, and as much body as anyone, and I shall be as much king of my realm as any other man is of his; and being so I'd do as I liked, and doing as I liked I'd please myself, and pleasing myself I'd be content, and when one is content he has nothing more to wish for, and when one has nothing more to wish for there's an end of it. So let the county come, and God be with you, and let us see one another, as one blind man said to the other."
"That's not bad philosophy you're talking, Sancho," said the canon, "but for all that there's a good deal to be said on this matter of counties."

To which Don Quixote replied, "I don't know what more there is to be said; I only guide myself by the example set me by the great Amadis of Gaul, when he made his squire count of Insula Firme. So, without any scruples of conscience, I can make a count of Sancho Panza, for he is one of the best squires that any knight-errant ever had."

The canon was astonished at the methodical nonsense (if nonsense can be methodical) that Don Quixote uttered, at the way he had described the adventure of the knight of the lake, at the impression the deliberate lies of the books he had read had made on him, and finally he marvelled at the simplicity of Sancho, who longed so eagerly to obtain the county his master had promised him.

By this time the canon's servants, who had gone to the inn to fetch the sumpter mule, had returned, and making a carpet and the green grass of the meadow serve as a table, they sat down in the shade of some trees and ate their meal there, so the carter wouldn't be deprived of the advantage of the spot, as has already been said. While they were eating they suddenly heard a loud noise and the sound of a bell that seemed to come from among some brambles and thick bushes close by, and the same instant they saw a beautiful goat, spotted all over black, white, and brown, spring out of the thicket with a goatherd after her, calling and using the usual cries to make her stop or turn back to the fold. The runaway goat, scared and frightened, ran towards the company as if seeking their protection and then stood still. The goatherd, coming up, seized her by the horns and began to talk to her as if she were endowed with reason and understanding: "Ah wanderer, wanderer, Spotty, Spotty — how have you gone limping all this time? What wolves have frightened you, my daughter? Won't you tell me what's the matter, my beauty? But what else can it be except that you are a female and can't keep still? A plague on your humours and the humours of those you take after! Come back, come back, my darling; and if you won't be so happy, at least you'll be safe in the fold or with your companions; for if you, who ought to keep and lead them, go wandering astray, what will become of them?"

The goatherd's talk amused all who heard it, but especially the canon, who said to him, "As you live, brother, take it easy, and don't be in such a hurry to drive this goat back to the fold; for, being female, as you say, she'll follow her natural instinct in spite of anything you can do to prevent it. Take this morsel and have a drink, and that will soothe your annoyance, and meanwhile the goat will rest." Saying this, he handed him the loins of a cold rabbit on a fork.

The goatherd took it with thanks, drank and calmed himself, and then said, "I should be sorry if your worships took me for a simpleton for having spoken so seriously to this animal; but the truth is there's a certain mystery in the words I used. I'm a country fellow, but not so much of one that I don't know how to deal with men and beasts."
"That I can well believe," said the curate, "for I know from experience that the woods breed men of learning, and shepherds' huts harbour philosophers."

"At any rate, señor," returned the goatherd, "they shelter men of experience; and so you may see the truth of this and grasp it, though I may seem to put myself forward without being asked, I will, if it doesn't tire you, gentlemen, and you will give me your attention for a little, tell you a true story that will confirm this gentleman's word" — and he pointed to the curate — "as well as my own."

To this Don Quixote replied, "Seeing that this affair has a certain colour of chivalry about it, I for my part, brother, will hear you most gladly, and so will all these gentlemen, from the high intelligence they possess and their love of curious novelties that interest, charm, and entertain the mind, as I'm sure your story will do. So begin, friend, for we are all ready to listen."

"I draw my stakes," said Sancho, "and will retreat with this pasty to the brook over there, where I mean to provision myself for three days; for I have heard my lord, Don Quixote, say that a knight-errant's squire should eat until he can hold no more, whenever he gets the chance — because it often happens that they accidentally get into a wood so thick they cannot find their way out of it for six days; and if the man isn't well filled or his saddle-bags well stocked, there he may stay, as very often he does, turned into a dried mummy."

"You're in the right of it, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "go where you will and eat all you can, for I have had enough, and only want to give my mind its refreshment, as I shall by listening to this good fellow's story."
"That's what we'll all do," said the canon; and then he asked the goatherd to begin the promised tale.

The goatherd gave the goat which he was holding by the horns a couple of slaps on the back, saying, "Lie down here beside me, Spotty, we have time enough to get back to our fold." The goat seemed to understand him, for as her master sat down she stretched herself quietly beside him and looked up in his face to show him she was all attention to what he was about to say; and then in these words he began his story.

title: Part 1, Chapter 51
paragraphs: What the goatherd told the people who were carrying Don Quixote away

Three leagues from this valley there is a village which, small as it is, ranks among the richest in this whole region. In it lived a farmer, a thoroughly decent man, and so widely respected that, although respect comes naturally to anyone who is rich, he was honored even more for his virtue than for the wealth he had built up. But what made him luckier still, by his own account, was having a daughter of such extraordinary beauty, rare intelligence, charm, and goodness that everyone who knew her or laid eyes on her marveled at the remarkable gifts heaven and nature had given her. She was beautiful as a child, she kept growing more beautiful, and by the age of sixteen she was utterly lovely. Word of her beauty began to spread through all the surrounding villages—but why do I say only the surrounding villages, when it traveled to distant cities, and even found its way into royal halls and reached the ears of people of every rank, who came from every direction to see her, as if they were coming to see some rare curiosity or a miracle-working image?

Her father guarded her, and she guarded herself; no locks, guards, or bolts protect a young woman better than her own modesty. The father's wealth and the daughter's beauty drew many men, neighbors and strangers alike, to ask for her hand in marriage. But he—as anyone might be who held the fate of so precious a jewel in his hands—was torn, unable to decide which of her countless suitors he should give her to. I was one of the many who felt that very natural desire, and since her father knew who I was, and I came from the same town, of untainted blood, in the prime of life, and very rich in property, I had high hopes of succeeding. There was another man from the same place with the same qualifications who was also courting her, and that left her father's decision hanging in the balance, because he felt his daughter would be well matched with either of us. So to get out of this dilemma he decided to put the question to Leandra—for that is the name of the wealthy young woman who has reduced me to misery—reasoning that since we were both equals, it was best to let his beloved daughter choose according to her own preference. It is an approach worth copying by every father who wants to settle his children in life. I don't mean they should let their children pick something worthless and bad, but that they should set good options before them and then let them choose freely among the good. I don't know which of us Leandra chose; I only know that her father put us both off, citing his daughter's tender age and using vague words that neither committed him nor dismissed us. My rival is named Anselmo, and I am Eugenio—so that you know the names of the characters in this tragedy, whose ending is still undecided, though it is obvious it must be a disaster.

Around this time a man named Vicente de la Roca arrived in our town, the son of a poor peasant from that same town. This Vicente was coming back from serving as a soldier in Italy and various other places. A captain who happened to pass through with his company had taken him from our village when he was a boy of about twelve, and now, twelve years later, the young man returned in a soldier's uniform, decked out in a thousand colors and covered with glass trinkets and fine steel chains. Today he would show up in one flashy outfit, tomorrow in another—but all of it cheap and gaudy, of little substance and less value. The peasants, who are malicious by nature and can be malice itself when they have nothing to do, noticed all this. They took inventory of his finery and his jewelry piece by piece and discovered that he owned three suits in different colors, with matching garters and stockings; but he worked up so many arrangements and combinations out of them that if they hadn't actually counted, anyone would have sworn he had paraded more than ten suits of clothes and twenty plumes. Don't treat everything I'm telling you about the clothes as irrelevant or padded out, because they play a major part in this story. He used to sit on a bench under the big poplar in our plaza, and there he would keep us all hanging open-mouthed on the stories he told about his exploits. There was no country on the face of the earth he hadn't seen, no battle he hadn't fought in; he had killed more Moors than there are in Morocco and Tunis, and fought more single combats—by his own account—than Garcilaso, Diego García de Paredes, and a thousand others he named, and he had come out of all of them victorious without losing a single drop of blood. Then again, he showed off marks of wounds which, though no one could make them out, he claimed were gunshot wounds received in various skirmishes and actions. Finally, with breathtaking arrogance, he addressed his equals as "you"—even people who knew exactly what he was—and declared that his right arm was his father and his deeds were his pedigree, and that as a soldier he was as good as the king himself. On top of all this swagger, he was a bit of a musician and strummed the guitar with such flair that some people said he made it talk; and his talents didn't stop there, because he was also something of a poet, and he would compose a ballad a league long about every little thing that happened in the town.

This soldier, then, whom I have just described—this Vicente de la Roca, this tough, this dandy, this musician, this poet—was often seen and watched by Leandra from a window of her house that overlooked the plaza. The glitter of his flashy clothes caught her eye, his ballads cast a spell on her (he handed out twenty copies of every one he wrote), and the tales of his exploits that he spread about himself reached her ears. In short—the devil must surely have arranged it—she fell in love with him before he had even presumed to think of courting her. And since no love affair comes off more easily than one that has the lady's own inclination as its ally, Leandra and Vicente reached an understanding without any trouble. Before any of her many suitors had the slightest suspicion of her plan, she had already carried it out: she left the house of her dearly loved father (she had no mother) and vanished from the village with the soldier, who came out of this adventure more triumphantly than out of any of the great number he boasted of. The whole village, and everyone who heard about it, was stunned by the affair. I was aghast, Anselmo thunderstruck, her father overwhelmed with grief, her relatives outraged, the authorities in an uproar, the officers of the Brotherhood under arms. They combed the roads, they searched the woods and everywhere else, and at the end of three days they found the wayward Leandra in a mountain cave, stripped down to her shift and robbed of all the money and precious jewels she had taken from home with her.

They brought her back to her devastated father and questioned her about her misfortune. She admitted without any pressure that Vicente de la Roca had deceived her: under a promise of marriage he had persuaded her to leave her father's house, saying he would take her to the richest and most delightful city in the whole world, which was Naples. She, badly advised and deluded, had believed him, robbed her father, and handed everything over to him the night she disappeared; and he had carried her off to a rugged mountain and shut her up in the cave where they found her. She also said that the soldier, without robbing her of her honor, had taken everything she had and gone off, leaving her in the cave—something that surprised everyone even more. It wasn't easy for us to believe in the young man's restraint, but she insisted on it so earnestly that it helped console her grieving father, who counted everything that had been taken as nothing, since his daughter had been left with the one jewel that, once lost, can never be recovered. The same day Leandra reappeared, her father removed her from our sight and took her away to shut her up in a convent in a town near here, hoping that time will wear away some of the disgrace she has brought on herself. Leandra's youth offered an excuse for her fault, at least among people who had no stake in whether she was good or bad; but those who knew her sharpness and intelligence didn't put her misstep down to ignorance, but to recklessness and to the natural disposition of women, which is for the most part flighty and unsteady.

With Leandra out of sight, Anselmo's eyes went blind—or at least found nothing to look at that gave them any pleasure—and mine were in darkness, without one ray of light to point them toward anything enjoyable while Leandra was gone. Our sadness deepened, our patience wore thin; we cursed the soldier's finery and railed against the carelessness of Leandra's father. In the end Anselmo and I agreed to leave the village and come to this valley, where—he grazing a large flock of his own sheep, and I a big herd of my own goats—we spend our lives among the trees, giving vent to our sorrows, sometimes singing the lovely Leandra's praises together, sometimes reproaching her, or else sighing alone and pouring out our complaints to heaven in solitude. Following our example, many more of Leandra's admirers have come to these wild mountains and taken up our way of life, and they are so numerous that you would think the place had been turned into the pastoral Arcadia, it is so full of shepherds and sheepfolds; there is not a spot in it where you don't hear the name of the lovely Leandra. Here one man curses her and calls her capricious, fickle, and shameless; there another condemns her as weak and frivolous; this one pardons and absolves her, that one rejects and reviles her; one praises her beauty, another tears apart her character. In short, they all abuse her and they all adore her, and this collective madness has gone so far that some complain of her scorn without ever having exchanged a word with her, and some even moan and grieve under the raging fever of jealousy, though she never gave anyone cause for it—because, as I've already said, her misconduct became known before her passion did. There is no crevice in the rocks, no streamside, no patch of shade under the trees that isn't occupied by some shepherd telling his troubles to the wind; wherever there is an echo, it repeats the name of Leandra. The mountains ring with "Leandra," the brooks murmur "Leandra," and Leandra keeps us all dazed and bewitched, hoping without hope and fearing without knowing what we fear. Of this whole foolish crowd, the one who shows the least sense and also the most is my rival Anselmo, because although he has so many other things to complain about, he complains only of separation; and to the accompaniment of a rebeck, which he plays admirably, he sings his complaints in verses that show real ingenuity. I follow another course—easier, and in my view wiser—which is to rail against the frivolity of women, their inconstancy, their double-dealing, their broken promises, their abandoned pledges, and, in short, the lack of judgment they show in placing their affections and attachments. This, gentlemen, was the reason for the words and remarks I aimed at this goat when I came up just now: since she's a female, I hold her in contempt, even though she is the best in my whole herd. That is the story I promised to tell you, and if I've been long-winded in telling it, I won't be slow in serving you. My hut is nearby, and I have fresh milk and delicious cheese there, along with a variety of appetizing fruit, as pleasing to the eye as to the palate.

title: Part 1, Chapter 52
paragraphs: About the quarrel Don Quixote had with the goatherd, together with the rare adventure of the penitents, which he brought to a happy conclusion at the cost of a great deal of sweat

The goatherd's tale pleased everyone who heard it, and the canon especially enjoyed it: he had noted with particular attention the manner in which it had been told, which was as unlike that of a clownish goatherd as it was like that of a polished city wit; and he remarked that the curate had been quite right to say that the woods bred men of learning. They all offered their services to Eugenio, but the one who proved most generous in this way was Don Quixote, who said to him, "Most assuredly, brother goatherd, if I were in any position to undertake an adventure, I would, this very instant, set out on your behalf, and would rescue Leandra from that convent (where she is no doubt held against her will), in spite of the abbess and all who might try to prevent me, and would put her into your hands to deal with as you saw fit — observing, however, the laws of chivalry, which lay down that no violence of any kind is to be offered to any maiden. But I trust in God our Lord that the might of one malign enchanter may not prove so great that the power of another, better disposed, cannot prove superior to it; and then I promise you my support and assistance, as I am bound to do by my profession, which is none other than to give aid to the weak and needy."

The goatherd looked him over, and noticing Don Quixote's sorry appearance and looks, was struck with wonder, and asked the barber, who was next to him, "Señor, who is this man who cuts such a figure and talks in such a way?"

"Who should it be," said the barber, "but the famous Don Quixote of La Mancha, the undoer of injustice, the righter of wrongs, the protector of damsels, the terror of giants, and the winner of battles?"

"That," said the goatherd, "sounds like what one reads in the books about knights-errant, who did everything you say this man does; though it's my belief that either you're joking, or this gentleman has empty rooms in his head."

"You're a great scoundrel," said Don Quixote, "and it's you who are empty and a fool. I am fuller than the whoreson bitch that bore you ever was;" and passing from words to deeds, he snatched up a loaf that lay near him and flung it full in the goatherd's face, with such force that he flattened his nose. The goatherd, who did not understand jokes and found himself roughly handled in such earnest, paid no respect to carpet, tablecloth, or diners. He sprang on Don Quixote, seized him by the throat with both hands, and would no doubt have throttled him, had not Sancho Panza come to the rescue that very instant. Sancho grasped him by the shoulders and flung him down on the table, smashing plates, breaking glasses, and upsetting and scattering everything on it. Don Quixote, finding himself free, tried to get on top of the goatherd, who, his face covered in blood and well kicked by Sancho, was on all fours feeling about for one of the table-knives to take a bloody revenge with. The canon and the curate, however, prevented him; but the barber so contrived it that he got Don Quixote under him, and rained down on him such a shower of fists that the poor knight's face streamed with blood as freely as the goatherd's own. The canon and the curate were bursting with laughter, the officers were capering with delight, and both parties hissed the fighters on as people do dogs worrying each other in a fight. Sancho alone was frantic, for he could not free himself from the grip of one of the canon's servants, who kept him from going to his master's aid.

At last, while everyone except the two bruisers mauling each other was in high glee, they heard a trumpet sound a note so doleful that it made them all look in the direction the sound seemed to come from. The one most stirred by it was Don Quixote, who, much against his will, was under the goatherd and something more than thoroughly pummelled. He said to him, "Brother devil — for it can't be anything else, since you've had the might and strength to overcome me — I beg you to agree to a truce for just one hour; the solemn note of that trumpet seems to me to summon me to some new adventure." The goatherd, who was by this time tired of pummelling and being pummelled, released him at once, and Don Quixote rose to his feet and turned his eyes toward the quarter from which the sound had come. There he suddenly saw, coming down the slope of a hill, several men dressed in white like penitents.

The fact was that the clouds had that year withheld their moisture from the earth, and in every village of the district they were organising processions, rogations, and penances, begging God to open the hand of his mercy and send rain; and to this end the people of a nearby village were going in procession to a holy hermitage that stood on one side of the valley. When Don Quixote saw the strange dress of the penitents, without stopping to think how often he had seen it before, he took it into his head that this was an adventure, and that it fell to him alone, as a knight-errant, to engage in it. He was all the more confirmed in this notion by the idea that an image draped in black they carried with them must be some illustrious lady whom these villains and discourteous thieves were carrying off by force. The moment this occurred to him, he ran with all speed to Rocinante, who was grazing at large, took the bridle and the buckler from the saddle-bow, had him bridled in an instant, called to Sancho for his sword, mounted Rocinante, braced his buckler on his arm, and in a loud voice exclaimed to those standing by, "Now, noble company, you shall see how important it is that there should be knights in the world professing the order of knight-errantry; now, I say, you shall see, by the deliverance of that worthy lady carried captive there, whether knights-errant deserve to be held in esteem." Saying this, he set his legs to Rocinante — he had no spurs — and at a full canter (for in all this veracious history we never read of Rocinante actually galloping) set off to meet the penitents, though the curate, the canon, and the barber ran to stop him. But it was not in their power, nor did he even halt at the shouts of Sancho, who called after him, "Where are you going, Señor Don Quixote? What devils have possessed you to set you on against our Catholic faith? Plague take me! Mind, that's a procession of penitents, and the lady they're carrying on that stand is the blessed image of the immaculate Virgin. Take care what you're doing, señor, for this time it may safely be said you don't know what you're about." Sancho's labour was wasted, for his master was so set on coming to blows with these sheeted figures and freeing the lady in black that he did not hear a word; and even if he had heard, he would not have turned back if the king himself had ordered it. He came up with the procession and reined in Rocinante — who was anxious enough already to slacken a little — and in a hoarse, excited voice exclaimed, "You who hide your faces — perhaps because you are not good subjects — pay attention and listen to what I am about to say to you." The first to halt were those carrying the image, and one of the four ecclesiastics chanting the Litany, struck by Don Quixote's strange figure, Rocinante's leanness, and the other ridiculous details he noticed, replied, "Brother, if you have anything to say to us, say it quickly, for these brethren are whipping themselves, and we can't stop, nor is it reasonable that we should stop to hear anything, unless it is short enough to be said in two words."

"I will say it in one," replied Don Quixote, "which is this: that you release this very instant that fair lady whose tears and sad face show plainly that you are carrying her off against her will, and that you have committed some outrage against her. I, who was born into the world to redress all such wrongs, will not allow you to advance one more step until you have restored to her the liberty she longs for and deserves."

From these words all the hearers concluded he must be a madman, and began to laugh heartily; and their laughter worked on Don Quixote's fury like gunpowder. Without another word he drew his sword and rushed at the stand. One of the bearers, leaving the burden to his comrades, came out to meet him, brandishing a forked stick he used to prop the stand up while resting. With it he caught a mighty cut Don Quixote aimed at him, which sliced the stick in two; but with the portion left in his hand he dealt such a thwack on the shoulder of Don Quixote's sword arm — which the buckler could not protect against the clownish blow — that poor Don Quixote came to the ground in a sad state.

Sancho Panza, coming up close behind, puffing and blowing, saw him fall and shouted to the assailant not to strike him again, for he was a poor enchanted knight who had never harmed anyone in his life. But what checked the clown was not Sancho's shouting; it was seeing that Don Quixote didn't stir hand or foot. Thinking he had killed him, he hastily hitched his tunic up under his belt and took off across the country like a deer.

By this time all of Don Quixote's companions had come up to where he lay. But the processionists, seeing them running up, and with them the officers of the Brotherhood with their crossbows, anticipated trouble. They clustered round the image, raised their hoods, and gripped their scourges, while the priests gripped their tapers, and awaited the attack, resolved to defend themselves and even to go on the offensive if they could. Fortune, however, arranged things better than they expected, for all Sancho did was throw himself on his master's body, raising over him the most doleful and laughable lamentation ever heard, for he believed his master was dead. The curate was known to another curate walking in the procession, and their recognising each other put both parties' fears to rest. The first told the other in two words who Don Quixote was, and he and the whole troop of penitents went to see if the poor gentleman was dead, and heard Sancho Panza saying, with tears in his eyes, "Oh flower of chivalry, who with one blow of a stick has ended the course of your well-spent life! Oh pride of your race, honour and glory of all La Mancha — no, of all the world, which for lack of you will be full of evildoers, no longer in fear of punishment for their crimes! Oh you, more generous than all the Alexanders, since for only eight months of service you gave me the best island the sea girds or surrounds! Humble with the proud, haughty with the humble, brave in the face of danger, patient under outrage, in love for no good reason, imitator of the good, scourge of the wicked, enemy of the mean — in short, knight-errant, which is all that can be said!"

At Sancho's cries and moans, Don Quixote came to himself, and the first thing he said was, "He who lives parted from you, sweetest Dulcinea, has miseries to endure greater than these. Help me, friend Sancho, to mount the enchanted cart, for I am in no condition to press the saddle of Rocinante — this shoulder is all in pieces."

"That I will do with all my heart, señor," said Sancho; "and let us go back to our village with these gentlemen, who wish you well, and there we will prepare for another sally, which may turn out more profitable and creditable for us."
"You're right, Sancho," replied Don Quixote; "it will be wise to let the malign influence of the stars now ruling us pass off."

The canon, the curate, and the barber told him he would be acting very wisely in doing as he said. So, highly amused at Sancho Panza's simplicities, they put Don Quixote in the cart as before. The procession formed itself in order again and went on its way; the goatherd took his leave of the party; the officers of the Brotherhood declined to go any farther, and the curate paid them what was due to them; the canon asked the curate to let him know how Don Quixote got on, whether he was cured of his madness or still suffered from it, and then asked leave to continue his journey. In short, they all separated and went their ways, leaving on their own the curate and the barber, Don Quixote, Sancho Panza, and the good Rocinante, who took everything with as much resignation as his master. The carter yoked his oxen and made Don Quixote comfortable on a truss of hay, and at his usual deliberate pace took the road the curate directed, and at the end of six days they reached Don Quixote's village. They entered it about the middle of the day, which happened to be a Sunday, and the people were all in the plaza, through which Don Quixote's cart passed. They all flocked to see what was in the cart, and when they recognised their townsman they were filled with amazement, and a boy ran off to bring the news to the housekeeper and the niece that their master and uncle had come back lean and yellow and laid out on a truss of hay on an ox-cart. It was piteous to hear the cries the two good women raised, how they beat their breasts and poured out fresh curses on those accursed books of chivalry — all of which they renewed when they saw Don Quixote coming in at the gate.

At the news of Don Quixote's arrival, Sancho Panza's wife came running, for by now she knew that her husband had gone away with him as his squire; and on seeing Sancho the first thing she asked him was whether the ass was well. Sancho replied that he was — better than his master.
"Thanks be to God," she said, "for being so good to me; but now tell me, my friend, what have you made by your squiring? What gown have you brought me back? What shoes for your children?"
"I bring nothing of that sort, wife," said Sancho; "though I bring other things of more consequence and value."

"I am very glad of that," his wife replied; "show me these things of more value and consequence, my friend; for I want to see them, to cheer a heart that has been so sad and heavy all this time you've been away."

"I'll show them to you at home, wife," said Sancho; "be content for now. If it please God that we should go out on our travels again in search of adventures, you'll soon see me a count, or governor of an island — and not one of those everyday ones either, but the best to be had."
"Heaven grant it, husband," she said, "for we have need of it. But tell me, what's this about islands? I don't understand it."
"Honey is not for the mouth of the ass," replied Sancho; "all in good time you shall see, wife — indeed, you'll be surprised to hear all your vassals call you 'your ladyship.'"

"What are you talking about, Sancho — with your ladyships, islands, and vassals?" returned Teresa Panza (for that was Sancho's wife's name, though they were not relations: in La Mancha it is customary for wives to take their husbands' surnames).

"Don't be in such a hurry to know all this, Teresa," said Sancho; "it's enough that I'm telling you the truth, so shut your mouth. But I may tell you this much in passing: that there's nothing in the world more delightful than to be a person of consequence, squire to a knight-errant, and a seeker of adventures. To be sure, most of those one runs into don't end as pleasantly as one would wish — out of a hundred, ninety-nine will turn out cross and contrary. I know it from experience, for I came out of some blanketed, and out of others belaboured. Still, for all that, it's a fine thing to be on the lookout for what may happen — crossing mountains, searching woods, climbing rocks, visiting castles, putting up at inns — all at free quarters, and devil a maravedi to pay."

While this conversation passed between Sancho Panza and his wife, Don Quixote's housekeeper and niece took him in, undressed him, and laid him in his old bed. He eyed them sideways and could not make out where he was. The curate charged the niece to be very careful to make her uncle comfortable, and to keep a watch over him so that he wouldn't slip away from them again, telling her what they had been obliged to do to bring him home. On hearing this, the pair once more lifted up their voices and renewed their curses on the books of chivalry, and begged heaven to plunge the authors of such lies and nonsense into the depths of the bottomless pit. They were, in short, kept in anxiety and dread that their uncle and master would give them the slip the moment he was a little better — and, as they feared, so it turned out.

But the author of this history, though he has devoted research and industry to uncovering the deeds Don Quixote achieved in his third sally, has been unable to obtain any information about them, at least from authentic documents. Tradition has merely preserved in the memory of La Mancha the fact that Don Quixote, the third time he sallied forth from home, made his way to Saragossa, where he attended some famous jousts held in that city, and that he had adventures there worthy of his valour and his high intelligence. Of his end and death he could find no particulars, and would not have ascertained or known of it, if good fortune had not produced for him an old physician who had in his possession a leaden box, which, by his account, had been discovered among the crumbling foundations of an ancient hermitage that was being rebuilt. In the box were found certain parchment manuscripts in Gothic script, but in Castilian verse, containing many of Don Quixote's exploits and setting forth the beauty of Dulcinea, the form of Rocinante, the fidelity of Sancho Panza, and the burial of Don Quixote himself, together with various epitaphs and eulogies on his life and character. But all that could be read and deciphered were the verses the trustworthy author of this new and unparalleled history now presents. And the said author asks of those who read it nothing in return for the great toil it has cost him in examining and searching the archives of La Mancha to bring it to light, save that they grant him the same credit thoughtful people give to the books of chivalry that have spread through the world and are so popular; for with this he will consider himself amply paid and fully satisfied, and will be encouraged to seek out and produce other histories — if not as truthful, at least equal in invention and no less entertaining. The first words written on the parchment found in the leaden box were these:
THE ACADEMICIANS OF ARGAMASILLA, A VILLAGE OF LA MANCHA, ON THE LIFE AND DEATH OF DON QUIXOTE OF LA MANCHA, HOC SCRIPSERUNT MONICONGO, ACADEMICIAN OF ARGAMASILLA, ON THE TOMB OF DON QUIXOTE
EPITAPH

The scatterbrain that gave La Mancha more / Rich spoils than Jason's; who a point so keen / Had to his wit, and happier far had been / If his wit's weathercock a blunter bore; / The arm renowned far as Gaeta's shore, / Cathay, and all the lands that lie between; / The muse discreet and terrible in mien / As ever wrote on brass in days of yore; / He who surpassed the Amadises all, / And who as naught the Galaors accounted, / Supported by his love and gallantry: / Who made the Belianises sing small, / And sought renown on Rocinante mounted; / Here, underneath this cold stone, doth he lie.
PANIAGUADO, ACADEMICIAN OF ARGAMASILLA, IN LAUDEM DULCINEAE DEL TOBOSO
SONNET

She, whose full features may be here descried, / High-bosomed, with a bearing of disdain, / Is Dulcinea, she for whom in vain / The great Don Quixote of La Mancha sighed. / For her, Toboso's queen, from side to side / He traversed the grim sierra, the champaign / Of Aranjuez, and Montiel's famous plain: / On Rocinante oft a weary ride. / Malignant planets, cruel destiny, / Pursued them both, the fair Manchegan dame, / And the unconquered star of chivalry. / Nor youth nor beauty saved her from the claim / Of death; he paid love's bitter penalty, / And left the marble to preserve his name.
CAPRICHOSO, A MOST ACUTE ACADEMICIAN OF ARGAMASILLA, IN PRAISE OF ROCINANTE, STEED OF DON QUIXOTE OF LA MANCHA
SONNET

On that proud throne of diamantine sheen, / Which the blood-reeking feet of Mars degrade, / The mad Manchegan's banner now hath been / By him in all its bravery displayed. / There hath he hung his arms and trenchant blade / Wherewith, achieving deeds till now unseen, / He slays, lays low, cleaves, hews; but art hath made / A novel style for our new paladin. / If Amadis be the proud boast of Gaul, / If by his progeny the fame of Greece / Through all the regions of the earth be spread, / Great Quixote crowned in grim Bellona's hall / To-day exalts La Mancha over these, / And above Greece or Gaul she holds her head. / Nor ends his glory here, for his good steed / Doth Brillador and Bayard far exceed; / As mettled steeds compared with Rocinante, / The reputation they have won is scanty.
BURLADOR, ACADEMICIAN OF ARGAMASILLA, ON SANCHO PANZA
SONNET

The worthy Sancho Panza here you see; / A great soul once was in that body small, / Nor was there squire upon this earthly ball / So plain and simple, or of guile so free. / Within an ace of being Count was he, / And would have been but for the spite and gall / Of this vile age, mean and illiberal, / That cannot even let a donkey be. / For mounted on an ass (excuse the word), / By Rocinante's side this gentle squire / Was wont his wandering master to attend. / Delusive hopes that lure the common herd / With promises of ease, the heart's desire, / In shadows, dreams, and smoke ye always end.
CACHIDIABLO, ACADEMICIAN OF ARGAMASILLA, ON THE TOMB OF DON QUIXOTE
EPITAPH

The knight lies here below, / Ill-errant and bruised sore, / Whom Rocinante bore / In his wanderings to and fro. / By the side of the knight is laid / Stolid man Sancho too, / Than whom a squire more true / Was not in the esquire trade.
TIQUITOC, ACADEMICIAN OF ARGAMASILLA, ON THE TOMB OF DULCINEA DEL TOBOSO
EPITAPH

Here Dulcinea lies. / Plump was she and robust: / Now she is ashes and dust: / The end of all flesh that dies. / A lady of high degree, / With the port of a lofty dame, / And the great Don Quixote's flame, / And the pride of her village was she.

These were all the verses that could be deciphered; the rest, the writing being worm-eaten, were handed over to one of the Academicians to make out the meaning conjecturally. We are told that, at the cost of many sleepless nights and much toil, he has succeeded, and that he means to publish them in hopes of Don Quixote's third sally.
_"Forse altro cantera con miglior plettro."_
Volume II
DEDICATION OF VOLUME II.
TO THE COUNT OF LEMOS:

A few days ago, when I sent Your Excellency my plays, which had appeared in print before being staged, I said, if I remember correctly, that Don Quixote was putting on his spurs to come and pay homage to Your Excellency. Now I say that "with his spurs on, he is on his way." If he reaches his destination, I think I shall have done some service to Your Excellency, as I am urged from many quarters to send him out, so as to dispel the disgust and revulsion caused by another Don Quixote who, under the name of Second Part, has gone masquerading through the world. The one who has shown the keenest longing for him is the great Emperor of China, who wrote me a letter in Chinese a month ago and sent it by special courier. He asked me — or rather, to tell the truth, begged me — to send him Don Quixote, for he intended to found a college where the Spanish tongue would be taught, and he wished the book to be read there to be the History of Don Quixote. He also added that I should go and be the rector of this college. I asked the bearer whether His Majesty had granted any sum toward my travel expenses. He answered, "No, not even in thought."

"Then, brother," I replied, "you can return to your China, post haste or at whatever pace you please, for I am not fit for so long a journey; and besides being ill, I am very short of money. Emperor for Emperor and Monarch for Monarch, I have at Naples the great Count of Lemos, who, without so many petty titles of colleges and rectorships, sustains me, protects me, and shows me more favour than I could wish for."

So I dismissed him, and now I take my leave of you, offering Your Excellency the "Trabajos de Persiles y Sigismunda," a book I shall finish within four months, Deo volente, and which will be either the worst or the best that has been composed in our language — I mean among those intended for entertainment; though I repent of having called it the worst, for, in the opinion of friends, it is bound to reach the height of possible quality. May Your Excellency return in such health as is wished for you; Persiles will be ready to kiss your hand, and I your feet, being, as I am, Your Excellency's most humble servant.
From Madrid, this last day of October of the year sixteen hundred and fifteen.
At the service of Your Excellency:
MIGUEL DE CERVANTES SAAVEDRA
THE AUTHOR'S PREFACE

God bless me, gentle (or perhaps plebeian) reader, how eagerly you must be looking forward to this preface, expecting to find in it retaliation, scolding, and abuse aimed at the author of the second Don Quixote — I mean the one who was, they say, begotten at Tordesillas and born at Tarragona! Well then, the truth is, I am not going to give you that satisfaction; for though injuries stir up anger in humbler breasts, in mine the rule must admit of an exception. You would have me call him an ass, a fool, and impudent, but I have no such intention; let his offence be its own punishment, with his bread let him eat it, and there's an end of it. What I can't help taking amiss is that he charges me with being old and one-handed — as if it had been in my power to keep time from passing over me, or as if the loss of my hand had been incurred in some tavern, and not on the grandest occasion the past or present has seen, or the future can hope to see. If my wounds have no beauty in the beholder's eye, they are at least honourable in the estimation of those who know where they were received; for the soldier shows to greater advantage dead in battle than alive in flight; and so strongly is this my feeling, that if it were now proposed to perform an impossibility for me, I would rather have had my share in that mighty action than be free of my wounds this minute without having been present at it. The wounds the soldier shows on his face and breast are stars that direct others to the heaven of honour and the ambition of merited praise. And besides, it is to be noted that one writes not with grey hairs but with the understanding, and the understanding commonly improves with years. I take it amiss, too, that he calls me envious and explains to me, as though I were ignorant, what envy is; for, really and truly, of the two kinds there are, I know only the one that is holy, noble, and high-minded; and if that is so, as it is, I am not likely to attack a priest, above all if, in addition, he holds the rank of familiar of the Holy Office. And if he said what he did on account of the person on whose behalf he seems to have spoken, he is entirely mistaken; for I worship that man's genius, and admire his works and his unceasing and strenuous industry. After all, I am grateful to this gentleman, the author, for saying that my novels are more satirical than exemplary, but that they are good; for they could not be that unless there was a little of everything in them.

I suspect you will say I am taking a very humble line and keeping myself too much within the bounds of moderation, out of a feeling that additional suffering should not be inflicted on a sufferer, and that what this gentleman has to endure must doubtless be very great, since he does not dare to come out into the open field in broad daylight but hides his name and disguises his country as if he had been guilty of lese majesty. If by chance you come to know him, tell him from me that I do not consider myself aggrieved; for I know well what the temptations of the devil are, and that one of the greatest is putting it into a man's head that he can write and print a book that will earn him as much fame as money, and as much money as fame; and to prove it, I beg you, in your own sprightly, pleasant way, to tell him this story.

There was a madman in Seville who fell into one of the drollest absurdities and habits any madman in the world ever fell into. It was this: he made a tube of reed, sharp at one end; and catching a dog in the street, or wherever, he held one of its legs fast with his foot, lifted up the other with his hand, fixed the tube as best he could in place, and by blowing made the dog as round as a ball. Then, holding it in this position, he gave it a couple of slaps on the belly and let it go, saying to the bystanders (and there were always plenty), "Do your worships think, now, that it's an easy thing to blow up a dog?" — Does your worship think now, that it's an easy thing to write a book?
And if this story doesn't suit him, you may, dear reader, tell him this one, which is also about a madman and a dog.

In Cordova there was another madman whose habit it was to carry a piece of marble slab or a stone — not the lightest — on his head, and when he came on any unwary dog he would draw close to it and let the weight fall right on top of it; on which the dog, in a rage, barking and howling, would run three streets without stopping. It happened, however, that one of the dogs he discharged his load on was a cap-maker's dog, of which the master was very fond. The stone came down hitting it on the head, the dog raised a yell at the blow, the master saw the affair and was furious, and snatching up a measuring-yard rushed at the madman and didn't leave a sound bone in his body — at every stroke he gave him he said, "You dog, you thief! my lurcher! Don't you see, you brute, that my dog is a lurcher?" And so, repeating the word "lurcher" again and again, he sent the madman away beaten to a jelly. The madman took the lesson to heart, and disappeared, and for more than a month never once showed himself in public; but after that he came out again with his old trick and a heavier load than ever. He approached a dog, and, examining it very carefully without venturing to drop the stone, said, "This is a lurcher; beware!" In short, every dog he came across, mastiff or terrier, he said was a lurcher, and he dropped no more stones. Maybe it will be the same with this historian: he will not venture another time to discharge the weight of his wit in books, which, being bad, are harder than stones. Tell him too that I don't care a farthing for the threat he holds out, of depriving me of my profit by means of his book; for, to borrow from the famous interlude of "The Perendenga," I say in answer, "Long life to my lord the Veintiquatro, and Christ be with us all." Long life to the great Conde de Lemos, whose Christian charity and well-known generosity support me against all the blows of my cursed fortune; and long life to the supreme benevolence of His Eminence of Toledo, Don Bernardo de Sandoval y Rojas; and what does it matter if there are no printing-presses in the world, or if they print more books against me than there are letters in the verses of Mingo Revulgo! These two princes, unsought by any flattery or adulation of mine, of their own goodness have taken it on themselves to show me kindness and protect me, and in this I consider myself happier and richer than if Fortune had raised me to her greatest height in the ordinary way. The poor man may keep his honour, but not the vicious; poverty may cast a cloud over nobility but cannot hide it altogether; and since virtue of itself sheds a certain light, even through the chinks of penury, it wins the esteem of lofty and noble spirits, and in consequence their protection. You need say no more to him, nor will I say anything more to you, except to ask you to bear in mind that this Second Part of "Don Quixote" which I offer you is cut by the same craftsman and from the same cloth as the First, and that in it I present you Don Quixote continued, and at length dead and buried, so that no one may dare bring forward any further evidence against him, for what has already been produced is sufficient; and suffice it, too, that some reputable person should have given an account of all these shrewd lunacies of his without going into the matter again, for abundance, even of good things, makes them less valued, and scarcity, even of what is bad, confers a certain value. I was forgetting to tell you that you may expect the "Persiles," which I am now finishing, and also the Second Part of "Galatea."

title: Part 2, Chapter 1
paragraphs: About the conversation the curate and the barber had with Don Quixote concerning his malady

Cide Hamete Benengeli relates, in the Second Part of this history covering Don Quixote's third expedition, that the curate and the barber went nearly a month without seeing him, for fear of stirring up his memory and bringing back to mind everything that had happened. Still, they did not fail to call on his niece and housekeeper, urging them to look after him carefully and to feed him comforting dishes, the kind good for the heart and the brain—since it was obvious that this was where all his trouble had its source. The niece and housekeeper answered that they were already doing exactly that, and intended to keep it up with every possible care and diligence, because they could see that their master was beginning, every now and then, to show signs of being in his right mind. The curate and the barber were greatly pleased by this, for it convinced them they had done the right thing in carrying him home enchanted on the ox-cart, as was recounted in the final chapter of the First Part of this history, as great as it is accurate. So they decided to pay him a visit and see for themselves how far he had improved, though they considered any real improvement nearly impossible; and they agreed between them not to raise any topic touching on knight-errantry, so as not to risk tearing open wounds that were still so fresh.

Accordingly they came to see him, and found him sitting up in bed wearing a green baize waistcoat and a red Toledo cap, looking so shrivelled and dried out that he might have been turned into a mummy. He welcomed them very warmly; they asked about his health, and he spoke about himself quite naturally and in very carefully chosen words. As the conversation went on, they drifted into discussing what people call statecraft and systems of government—correcting this abuse, condemning that one, reforming one custom and doing away with another—each of the three setting himself up as a fresh lawgiver, a modern Lycurgus or a brand-new Solon; and they overhauled the State so thoroughly that they might as well have thrown it into a furnace and pulled out something entirely different from what went in. On every subject they touched, Don Quixote spoke with such good sense that his two examiners felt entirely convinced he had recovered completely and was in full possession of his wits.

The niece and housekeeper were there during the conversation and could not thank God enough at seeing their master so clear-headed. The curate, however, abandoned his original plan of steering clear of anything to do with chivalry, and decided to put Don Quixote's recovery to a thorough test, to find out whether it was genuine or not. So, moving from one subject to the next, he came at last to the news arriving from the capital, and mentioned among other things that it was regarded as certain that the Turk was coming down with a powerful fleet, that nobody knew what his plans were or when the great storm would break, and that all of Christendom—which this threat calls to arms almost every year—was on edge about it; he added that his Majesty had already provided for the defense of the coasts of Naples and Sicily and the island of Malta.

Don Quixote answered, “His Majesty has acted like a prudent commander in seeing to the security of his realms in good time, so that the enemy will not catch him unprepared; but if anyone asked my advice, I would urge him to adopt a precaution that his Majesty, at this moment, is surely very far from contemplating.”

The instant the curate heard this, he said to himself, “God hold you in his hand, poor Don Quixote, for it seems to me you are plunging from the high peak of your madness straight down into the deep abyss of your simplicity.”

But the barber, who had formed the same suspicion as the curate, asked Don Quixote what this measure was that he thought ought to be adopted; perhaps, he said, it might turn out to be one more entry for the long list of useless proposals that people were forever pressing on princes.
“Mine, master shaver,” said Don Quixote, “will not be useless; on the contrary, it will be exactly to the point.”

“That isn't what I meant,” said the barber, “only that experience has shown that all, or most, of the schemes put before his Majesty are either impossible, or absurd, or harmful to the King and to the kingdom.”

“Mine, though,” Don Quixote replied, “is neither impossible nor absurd; it is the easiest, the most sensible, the quickest and most efficient plan that could ever occur to the mind of any deviser of projects.”
“You are taking your time getting to it, Señor Don Quixote,” said the curate.

“I have no wish to state it here and now,” said Don Quixote, “only to have it reach the ears of the lords of the council tomorrow morning, so that somebody else walks off with the thanks and the reward for my labor.”

“As for me,” said the barber, “I give my word, here and before God, that I will not repeat what your worship says to King, Rook, or any man on earth—an oath I picked up from the ballad of the curate who, in the opening verses, tipped off the king about the thief who had robbed him of his hundred gold crowns and his ambling mule.”
“I don't know my ballads,” said Don Quixote, “but I know the oath is a sound one, because I know the barber to be an honest man.”
“Even if he were not,” said the curate, “I will stand surety and vouch for him: in this affair he will be as silent as a mute, on pain of paying whatever penalty the court might hand down.”
“And who will vouch for you, señor curate?” said Don Quixote.
“My profession,” answered the curate, “which is the keeping of secrets.”

“God's body!” said Don Quixote at this, “what more does his Majesty need to do than command, by public proclamation, that all the knights-errant scattered across Spain assemble in the capital on an appointed day? Even if no more than half a dozen turn up, there may be one among them who, single-handed, would be enough to destroy the whole power of the Turk. Pay attention now and follow my reasoning. Is it anything new, I ask you, for a single knight-errant to cut down an army of two hundred thousand men, as if the whole lot of them shared a single throat or were made of sugar paste? Come, tell me—how many histories are crammed with marvels of exactly this kind? If only—to my misfortune, though I speak for no one else—the famous Don Belianis were alive today, or any one of the countless descendants of Amadis of Gaul! If any of those men were living now and came face to face with the Turk, I swear I would not bet much on the Turk's chances. But God will look after his people and will raise up someone who, if not as valiant as the knights-errant of old, will at least not fall short of them in spirit; God knows what I mean, and I will say no more.”

“Heaven help us!” the niece cried out at this, “strike me dead if my master isn't itching to turn knight-errant all over again!” To which Don Quixote replied, “A knight-errant I shall die, and the Turk may come down or go up whenever he pleases, and with all the force he can muster; once again I say, God knows what I mean.” At this point the barber spoke up: “I beg your worships' permission to tell a short story about something that happened in Seville—it fits the present moment so perfectly that I am longing to tell it.” Don Quixote gave him leave, the others settled in to listen, and he began like this:

“In the madhouse at Seville there was a man whose relatives had placed him there as being out of his mind. He had taken his degree in canon law at Osuna; though most people held that even if he had been a graduate of Salamanca, he would have been just as mad. After several years of confinement, this graduate got it into his head that he was sane and fully in his right mind, and on that conviction he wrote to the Archbishop, pleading earnestly and in very correct language to be released from the misery in which he was living, since by God's mercy he had now recovered his lost reason—though his relatives, wanting to enjoy his estate, kept him locked up, and in defiance of the truth would have him counted a madman to his dying day. The Archbishop, won over by a string of sensible, well-composed letters, instructed one of his chaplains to find out from the madhouse whether the licentiate's claims were true, to speak with the madman himself, and, if he appeared to be in his senses, to take him out and set him free. The chaplain did so, but the governor assured him that the man was still mad: although he often talked like a person of great intelligence, in the end he would erupt into nonsense that matched, in quantity and quality, all the sensible things he had said before—as anyone could easily test by talking with him. The chaplain decided to make the experiment, and being given access to the madman, he conversed with him for an hour or more, during which the man never said a single incoherent or absurd word; on the contrary, he spoke so rationally that the chaplain could not help believing him sane. Among other things, the man said the governor was working against him, unwilling to forfeit the gifts his relatives sent for reporting him still mad with only lucid intervals; and that the greatest enemy he had in his misfortune was his large fortune, since to go on enjoying it his enemies belittled and cast doubt on the mercy our Lord had shown him in turning him back from a brute beast into a man. In short, he spoke in such a way that the governor came under suspicion, his relatives looked grasping and heartless, and he himself appeared so reasonable that the chaplain resolved to take him along so the Archbishop could see him and judge the truth of the matter for himself. Acting on this conviction, the good chaplain asked the governor to have the clothes brought in which the licentiate had entered the house. Once more the governor warned him to watch what he was doing, since the licentiate was beyond any doubt still mad; but all his cautions and warnings could not dissuade the chaplain from taking the man away. Seeing it was the Archbishop's order, the governor complied, and they dressed the licentiate in his own clothes, which were new and respectable. The moment he saw himself dressed like a sane man and stripped of the look of a lunatic, he begged the chaplain, as an act of charity, to let him go and say goodbye to his comrades the madmen. The chaplain said he would go along to see what madmen the house contained; so they went upstairs, with several of those present following. Coming to a cage holding a raving madman—who happened just then to be calm and quiet—the licentiate said to him, ‘Brother, consider whether you have any errands for me, for I am going home. God, in his infinite goodness and mercy, has been pleased to give me back my reason, through no merit of my own. I am cured now and in my right mind, for with God's power nothing is impossible. Keep strong hope and trust in him, for as he has restored me to my former condition, so he will restore you too, if you trust in him. I will make a point of sending you some good things to eat; and be sure you eat them, because I want you to know that I am convinced, as one who has been through it, that all this madness of ours comes from having an empty stomach and a head full of wind. Take heart! Take heart! Losing courage in misfortune ruins the health and brings on death.'

“Every word the licentiate said was overheard by another madman in a cage opposite the raving one; and lifting himself off an old mat where he lay stark naked, he demanded in a loud voice to know who it was that was leaving cured and in his right mind. The licentiate answered, ‘It is I, brother, who am going; I no longer have any need to stay here, and for that I give infinite thanks to Heaven, which has shown me such great mercy.'
“‘Watch what you are saying, licentiate; don't let the devil trick you,' the madman replied. ‘Hold still, stay right where you are, and you will spare yourself the trouble of coming back.'
“‘I know I am cured,' the licentiate returned, ‘and I shall not have to make the rounds of penance again.'

“‘You, cured!' said the madman; ‘well, time will tell; God go with you; but I swear to you by Jupiter, whose majesty I represent on this earth, that for this one crime which Seville commits today—releasing you from this house and treating you as if you were sane—I am bound to visit a punishment on the city that will be remembered through all the ages, amen. Do you not know, you wretched little licentiate, that I can do it? For I am, as I say, Jupiter the Thunderer, holding in my hands the burning bolts with which I can threaten the world, and lay it waste, as is my custom. But I will punish this ignorant town in one way only: I will not rain upon it, nor on any part of its district or territory, for three full years, counted from the day and hour this threat is pronounced. You free, you cured, you in your right mind! and I mad, I deranged, I tied up! I would as soon think of sending rain as of hanging myself.'

“The bystanders stood listening to the madman's shouts and declarations; but our licentiate turned to the chaplain, gripped him by the hands, and said, ‘Don't be troubled, señor; pay no attention to what this madman has said; for if he is Jupiter and refuses to send rain, I, who am Neptune, the father and god of the waters, will rain whenever I please and whenever it is needed.'

“The governor and the onlookers burst out laughing, and their laughter left the chaplain half ashamed; he answered, ‘All the same, Señor Neptune, it will not do to annoy Señor Jupiter; stay where you are, and some other day, when the occasion is better and there is more time, we will come back for you.' So they stripped the licentiate, he remained where he was, and that is the end of the story.”

“So that is the story, master barber,” said Don Quixote, “the one that fit the moment so perfectly you simply had to tell it? Ah, master shaver, master shaver! how blind a man must be who cannot see through a sieve. Is it really possible you do not know that comparisons—of wit with wit, valor with valor, beauty with beauty, lineage with lineage—are always hateful and unwelcome? I, master barber, am not Neptune, god of the waters, nor do I ask anyone to take me for a clever man, because I am not one. My one ambition is to make the world see the mistake it makes in failing to revive that happy age when the order of knight-errantry rode the field. But our corrupt times do not deserve to enjoy the blessing those ages enjoyed, when knights-errant took upon their own shoulders the defense of kingdoms, the protection of damsels, the relief of orphans and wards, the punishment of the proud, and the reward of the humble. With most of the knights of today, what rustles as they move is the damask, brocade, and rich cloth they wear, not the chain mail of their armor. No knight nowadays sleeps in the open field, exposed to the rigor of the heavens, in full armor from head to foot; no one now snatches a doze, as they say, without taking his feet from the stirrups, propped on his lance, as the knights-errant used to do; no one now rides out of the forest, crosses those mountains yonder, and then walks the barren, lonely seashore—stormy and tempestuous as the sea usually is—and finding on the beach a small boat without oars, sail, mast, or rigging of any kind, with a fearless heart throws himself into it and gives himself over to the furious waves of the deep, which one moment lift him to the sky and the next drop him into the abyss; and setting his chest against the irresistible gale, finds himself, when he least expects it, three thousand leagues and more from the place where he set out, and leaping ashore in a remote and unknown land meets with adventures worthy of being written not on parchment but on bronze. Today, instead, sloth triumphs over effort, idleness over labor, vice over virtue, arrogance over courage, and the theory of arms over their practice—arms that lived and shone only in the golden ages and in the knights-errant. Tell me, if you can: who was more virtuous and more valiant than the famous Amadis of Gaul? Who more discreet than Palmerin of England? Who more affable and obliging than Tirante el Blanco? Who more courtly than Lisuarte of Greece? Who gave or took more sword-cuts than Don Belianis? Who more intrepid than Perion of Gaul? Who readier to face danger than Felixmarte of Hircania? Who more sincere than Esplandian? Who more impetuous than Don Cirongilio of Thrace? Who bolder than Rodamonte? Who more prudent than King Sobrino? Who more daring than Reinaldos? Who more invincible than Roland? And who more gallant and courteous than Ruggiero, from whom the present-day dukes of Ferrara descend, according to Turpin in his ‘Cosmography'? All these knights, and many more I could name, señor curate, were knights-errant, the light and glory of chivalry. Men like these, or men of their kind, are the ones I would want for my plan; with them, his Majesty would find himself well served and spared great expense, and the Turk would be left tearing out his beard.
