And so I will stay where I am, since the chaplain is not taking me away; and if Jupiter, as the barber has told us, will not send rain, here I stand, and I will rain whenever I feel like it. I say this so that Master Basin will know I understand him.”
“Truly, Señor Don Quixote,” said the barber, “I meant nothing of the kind; as God is my witness, my intention was good, and your worship has no cause to take offense.”
“Whether I have cause to take offense or not,” Don Quixote answered, “is something I can judge best myself.”

At this point the curate spoke up: “I have hardly said a word so far; and I would gladly be rid of a misgiving, raised by what Don Quixote has been saying, that gnaws at my conscience and gives it no rest.”
“The señor curate has leave for that and more,” Don Quixote returned, “so let him state his misgiving, for it is no pleasant thing to carry a doubt on one's conscience.”

“With that permission, then,” said the curate, “I confess my doubt is this: try as I may, I cannot bring myself to believe that the whole crowd of knights-errant your worship, Señor Don Quixote, has listed were ever truly persons of flesh and blood who actually lived in this world; on the contrary, I suspect the whole thing is fiction, fable, and falsehood—dreams recounted by men just waking from sleep, or rather still half asleep.”

“That is another error,” Don Quixote replied, “into which many have fallen who refuse to believe such knights ever existed; and on various occasions, with various people, I have tried to drag this nearly universal mistake into the light of truth. Sometimes I have failed in the attempt, and sometimes I have succeeded, propping it on the shoulders of the truth itself—a truth so plain that I could almost say I have seen Amadis of Gaul with my own eyes: a man of tall stature, fair complexion, with a handsome though black beard, his expression somewhere between gentle and stern; a man of few words, slow to anger and quick to put it aside. And just as I have sketched Amadis, so, I believe, I could paint and describe every knight-errant in all the histories of the world; for through my perception that they were exactly what their histories report, and through the deeds they performed and the characters they showed, one can deduce, with the help of sound philosophy, their features, their coloring, and their build.”
“How big, in your worship's judgment, must the giant Morgante have been, Señor Don Quixote?” asked the barber.

“On the question of giants,” Don Quixote answered, “opinions are divided over whether any ever existed in this world; but Holy Scripture, which cannot stray from the truth by so much as a jot, shows us that they did, when it gives us the story of that huge Philistine Goliath, who stood seven and a half cubits tall—an enormous height. In the island of Sicily, likewise, leg-bones and arm-bones have been dug up so large that their size proves their owners were giants, as tall as great towers; geometry puts the fact beyond dispute. Even so, I cannot say with certainty how big Morgante was, though I suspect he cannot have been especially tall; and what inclines me to this view is that in the history where his deeds are specially recorded, I find that he often slept under a roof, and since he found houses big enough to hold him, his bulk clearly cannot have been anything outlandish.”

“Quite right,” said the curate, who, surrendering to the pleasure of hearing such absurdities, asked him what he imagined the faces of Reinaldos of Montalban, Don Roland, and the rest of the Twelve Peers of France to have been like, since all of them were knights-errant.

“As for Reinaldos,” Don Quixote replied, “I would venture to say he was broad in the face, ruddy in complexion, with restless, somewhat bulging eyes, exceedingly touchy and quick to take offense, and fond of the company of thieves and ruffians. As for Roland—or Rotolando, or Orlando, for the histories give him all these names—I am of the opinion, and maintain, that he was of medium height, broad-shouldered, somewhat bow-legged, dark-skinned and red-bearded, with a hairy body and a threatening look; a man of few words, but very courteous and well-mannered.”

“If Roland was no more attractive a figure than your worship describes,” said the curate, “it is small wonder the fair Lady Angelica turned him down and abandoned him for the charm, sparkle, and wit of that downy-bearded young Moor to whom she gave herself; she showed good judgment in preferring the soft gentleness of Medoro to the roughness of Roland.”

“That Angelica, señor curate,” Don Quixote returned, “was a giddy young woman, flighty and rather wanton, and she left the world as full of her escapades as of the fame of her beauty. She spurned a thousand gentlemen, men of valor and intelligence, and settled for a smooth-cheeked slip of a page with neither fortune nor reputation—except whatever name for gratitude his devotion to his friend earned him. The great poet who sang her beauty, the famous Ariosto, having no wish to sing what happened to her after her disgraceful surrender—adventures which were probably none too respectable—dropped her with the lines:

How she came to receive the sceptre of Cathay,
some bard with a defter pen may sing one day;

and this turned out to be a kind of prophecy, since poets are also called _vates_, that is, diviners; and its truth was borne out, for since then a famous Andalusian poet has wept over and sung her tears, and another famous and exceptional poet, a Castilian, has sung her beauty.”
“Tell me, Señor Don Quixote,” the barber put in here, “among all those who praised her, has there never been a poet to write a satire against this Lady Angelica?”

“I can easily believe,” Don Quixote replied, “that if Sacripante or Roland had been poets, they would have given the young lady a proper dressing-down; for it is the natural habit of poets scorned and rejected by their ladies—whether imaginary or real, in short, by whomever they choose as mistresses of their thoughts—to avenge themselves with satires and lampoons: a revenge, certainly, unworthy of generous hearts. But to this day I have heard of no defamatory verse against the Lady Angelica, though she turned the world upside down.”

“Remarkable,” said the curate; but at that moment they heard the housekeeper and the niece, who had slipped out of the conversation earlier, shouting in the courtyard, and at the noise they all rushed out.

title: Part 2, Chapter 2
paragraphs: Which treats of the notable altercation Sancho Panza had with Don Quixote's niece and housekeeper, together with other droll matters

The history relates that the outcry Don Quixote, the curate, and the barber heard came from the niece and the housekeeper, who were shouting at Sancho — striving to bar the door against him as he tried to force his way in to see Don Quixote: "What does the vagabond want in this house? Be off to your own, brother, for it's you and no one else who deludes my master, and leads him astray, and takes him tramping about the country."

To which Sancho replied, "Devil's own housekeeper! It's I who am deluded, and led astray, and taken tramping about the country, not your master! He's carried me all over the world, and you're greatly mistaken. He enticed me away from home by a trick, promising me an island that I'm still waiting for."
"May evil islands choke you, you detestable Sancho," said the niece. "What are islands? Is it something to eat, glutton and gormandiser that you are?"
"It's not something to eat," replied Sancho, "but something to govern and rule — and better than four cities or four judgeships at court."
"For all that," said the housekeeper, "you don't come in here, you bag of mischief and sack of knavery; go govern your house and dig your seed-patch, and give over looking for islands or shy-lands."

The curate and the barber listened with great amusement to the words of the three; but Don Quixote, anxious lest Sancho blab and blurt out a whole heap of mischievous stupidities — touching on points that might not be altogether to his credit — called to him and made the other two hold their tongues and let him in. Sancho entered, and the curate and the barber took their leave of Don Quixote, of whose recovery they despaired when they saw how wedded he was to his crazy ideas and how saturated with the nonsense of his unlucky chivalry. Said the curate to the barber, "You'll see, gossip, that when we are least thinking of it, our gentleman will be off once more for another flight."

"I have no doubt of it," returned the barber; "but I don't wonder so much at the madness of the knight as at the simplicity of the squire, who has such a firm belief in all that about the island that I suppose no amount of exposure imaginable would get it out of his head."

"God help them," said the curate; "and let us be on the lookout to see what comes of all these absurdities of the knight and squire — for it seems as if they had both been cast in the same mould, and the madness of the master without the simplicity of the man would not be worth a farthing."
"That's true," said the barber, "and I would very much like to know what the pair are talking about at this moment."
"I promise you," said the curate, "the niece or the housekeeper will tell us by and by, for they're not the ones to forget to listen."

Meanwhile Don Quixote shut himself up in his room with Sancho, and when they were alone he said to him, "It grieves me greatly, Sancho, that you should have said, and still say, that I took you out of your cottage, when you know I did not stay in my own house. We sallied forth together, took the road together, wandered abroad together; we have had the same fortune and the same luck; if they blanketed you once, they belaboured me a hundred times, and that's the only advantage I have over you."
"That was only reasonable," replied Sancho, "for, by what your worship says, misfortunes belong more properly to knights-errant than to their squires."
"You are mistaken, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "according to the maxim _quando caput dolet_, etc."
"I don't understand any language but my own," said Sancho.

"I mean to say," said Don Quixote, "that when the head suffers, all the members suffer; and so, being your lord and master, I am your head, and you, being my servant, are a part of me; therefore any evil that affects, or shall affect, me should give you pain, and what affects you should give pain to me."

"It should be so," said Sancho, "but when I was blanketed as a member, my head was on the other side of the wall, looking on while I was flying through the air, and felt no pain whatever; and if the members are obliged to feel the suffering of the head, then the head should be obliged to feel theirs."

"Do you mean to say now, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that I felt nothing while they were blanketing you? If you do, you must not say so or think it, for I felt more pain then in spirit than you did in body. But let us put that aside for the present, for we shall have opportunities enough to consider and settle the point. Tell me, Sancho my friend, what do they say about me here in the village? What do the common people think of me? What do the hidalgos? What do the caballeros? What do they say of my valour; of my achievements; of my courtesy? How do they treat the task I have undertaken in reviving and restoring to the world the now forgotten order of chivalry? In short, Sancho, I would have you tell me everything that has come to your ears on this subject — and you are to tell me without adding anything to the good or taking anything from the bad; for it is the duty of loyal vassals to tell the truth to their lords just as it is and in its proper shape, neither letting flattery add to it nor any idle deference lessen it. And I would have you know, Sancho, that if the naked truth, undisguised by flattery, reached the ears of princes, times would be different, and other ages would be reckoned iron ages more than ours — which I hold to be the golden age of these latter days. Take the benefit of this advice, Sancho, and report to me clearly and faithfully the truth of what you know touching what I have asked of you."

"That I'll do with all my heart, master," replied Sancho, "provided your worship will not be vexed at what I say, since you wish me to say it out in all its nakedness, without putting any more clothes on it than it came to my knowledge in."
"I will not be vexed at all," returned Don Quixote; "you may speak freely, Sancho, without beating about the bush."

"Well then," he said, "first of all I have to tell you that the common people take your worship for a mighty great madman, and me for no less a fool. The hidalgos say that, not keeping within the bounds of your quality of gentleman, you've assumed the 'Don,' and made a knight of yourself at a jump, with four vine-stocks and a couple of acres of land and never a shirt to your back. The caballeros say they don't want to have hidalgos setting up in opposition to them, particularly squire hidalgos who polish their own shoes and darn their black stockings with green silk."
"That," said Don Quixote, "does not apply to me, for I always go well dressed and never patched; ragged I may be, but ragged more from the wear and tear of arms than of time."

"As to your worship's valour, courtesy, accomplishments, and task, there's a variety of opinions. Some say 'mad but droll'; others, 'valiant but unlucky'; others, 'courteous but meddling' — and then they go into such a number of things that they don't leave a whole bone in either your worship or myself."

"Recollect, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "that wherever virtue exists in any eminent degree, it is persecuted. Few or none of the famous men who have lived escaped being calumniated by malice. Julius Caesar, the boldest, wisest, and bravest of captains, was charged with being ambitious, and not particularly clean in his dress, or pure in his morals. Of Alexander, whose deeds won him the name of Great, they say he was something of a drunkard. Of Hercules, him of the many labours, it is said he was lewd and luxurious. Of Don Galaor, the brother of Amadis of Gaul, it was whispered that he was over-quarrelsome, and of his brother that he was lachrymose. So, O Sancho, amid all these calumnies against good men, mine may be let pass, since they are no more than what you have said."
"That's just where it is, body of my father!"
"Is there more, then?" asked Don Quixote.

"There's the tail to be skinned yet," said Sancho; "all so far is cakes and fancy bread. But if your worship wants to know all about the calumnies they bring against you, I'll fetch you one this instant who can tell you the whole of them without missing an atom; for last night the son of Bartholomew Carrasco, who has been studying at Salamanca, came home after being made a bachelor, and when I went to welcome him, he told me your worship's history is already abroad in books, with the title of THE INGENIOUS GENTLEMAN DON QUIXOTE OF LA MANCHA. And he says they mention me in it by my own name of Sancho Panza, and the lady Dulcinea del Toboso too, and various things that happened to us when we were alone — so much so that I crossed myself in wonder at how the historian who wrote them down could have known them."
"I promise you, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "the author of our history will be some sage enchanter; for to such, nothing they choose to write about is hidden."
"What!" said Sancho. "A sage and an enchanter! Why, the bachelor Samson Carrasco (that's the name of him I spoke of) says the author of the history is called Cide Hamete Berengena."
"That is a Moorish name," said Don Quixote.
"Maybe so," replied Sancho; "for I have heard say that the Moors are mostly great lovers of berengenas."
"You must have mistaken the surname of this 'Cide' — which means in Arabic 'Lord,' Sancho," observed Don Quixote.
"Very likely," replied Sancho, "but if your worship wishes me to fetch the bachelor, I'll go for him in a twinkling."
"You will do me a great pleasure, my friend," said Don Quixote, "for what you have told me has amazed me, and I shall not eat a morsel that will agree with me until I've heard all about it."
"Then I'm off for him," said Sancho; and leaving his master, he went in search of the bachelor, with whom he returned in a short time; and the three of them together had a very droll conversation.

title: Part 2, Chapter 3
paragraphs: About the laughable conversation that passed between Don Quixote, Sancho Panza, and the bachelor Samson Carrasco

Don Quixote sat deep in thought, waiting for the bachelor Carrasco, from whom he was to hear how he himself had been put into a book, as Sancho said. He could not persuade himself that any such history could exist, since the blood of the enemies he had slain was not yet dry on the blade of his sword, and now they wanted to make out that his mighty achievements were going about in print. All the same, he supposed that some sage, whether friend or enemy, might by the aid of magic have put them to press: a friend, in order to magnify and exalt them above the most famous ever achieved by any knight-errant; an enemy, to bring them to nothing and degrade them below the meanest ever recorded of any low squire — though, as he said to himself, the achievements of squires had never been recorded. If, however, it were a fact that such a history existed, then, being the story of a knight-errant, it must necessarily be grandiloquent, lofty, imposing, grand, and true. With this thought he comforted himself somewhat, though it made him uncomfortable to think the author was a Moor, judging by the title "Cide"; and that no truth was to be looked for from Moors, who are all impostors, cheats, and schemers. He was afraid the author might have dealt with his love affairs in some indecorous fashion, to the discredit and prejudice of the purity of his lady Dulcinea del Toboso; he would have had him set forth the fidelity and respect he had always shown her, spurning queens, empresses, and damsels of all sorts, and keeping in check the impetuosity of his natural impulses. Absorbed and wrapped up in these and various other thoughts, he was found by Sancho and Carrasco, whom Don Quixote received with great courtesy.

The bachelor, though he was called Samson, was of no great bodily size, but he was a very great wag; sallow-complexioned, but very sharp-witted, somewhere about twenty-four years of age, with a round face, a flat nose, and a large mouth — all signs of a mischievous disposition and a love of fun and jokes. He gave a sample of it as soon as he saw Don Quixote, by falling to his knees before him and saying, "Let me kiss your mightiness's hand, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha; for by the habit of St. Peter that I wear, though I have no more than the first four orders, your worship is one of the most famous knights-errant that have ever been, or ever will be, all the world over. A blessing on Cide Hamete Benengeli, who wrote the history of your great deeds, and a double blessing on the connoisseur who took the trouble to have it translated out of the Arabic into our Castilian vulgar tongue for the universal entertainment of the people!"
Don Quixote made him rise, and said, "So, then, it is true that there is a history of me, and that it was a Moor and a sage who wrote it?"

"So true is it, señor," said Samson, "that my belief is there are more than twelve thousand volumes of the said history in print this very day. Just ask Portugal, Barcelona, and Valencia, where they have been printed; and there is even a report that it is being printed at Antwerp, and I am persuaded there will not be a country or language in which there will not be a translation of it."

"One of the things," Don Quixote here observed, "that ought to give the greatest pleasure to a virtuous and eminent man is to find himself in his lifetime in print and in type, familiar in people's mouths with a good name — I say with a good name, for if it be the opposite, then no death is to be compared to it."

"If it goes by good name and fame," said the bachelor, "your worship alone bears away the palm from all the knights-errant; for the Moor in his own language, and the Christian in his, have taken care to set before us your gallantry, your high courage in facing dangers, your fortitude under adversity, your patience under misfortunes as well as wounds, the purity and continence of the platonic loves of your worship and my lady Doña Dulcinea del Toboso —"
"I never heard my lady Dulcinea called Doña," Sancho observed here. "Nothing more than the lady Dulcinea del Toboso; so here already the history is wrong."
"That's no objection of any importance," replied Carrasco.
"Certainly not," said Don Quixote; "but tell me, señor bachelor, what deeds of mine are they that are made most of in this history?"

"On that point," replied the bachelor, "opinions differ, as tastes do. Some swear by the adventure of the windmills that your worship took to be Briareuses and giants; others by that of the fulling mills; one cries up the description of the two armies that turned out to be two droves of sheep; another that of the dead body on its way to be buried at Segovia; a third says the freeing of the galley slaves is the best of all, and a fourth that nothing comes up to the affair with the Benedictine giants, and the battle with the valiant Biscayan."
"Tell me, señor bachelor," said Sancho at this point, "does the adventure with the Yanguesans come in, when our good Rocinante went hankering after dainties?"
"The sage has left nothing in the ink-bottle," replied Samson; "he tells everything and sets down every detail, even down to the capers worthy Sancho cut in the blanket."
"I cut no capers in the blanket," returned Sancho; "in the air I did, and more of them than I liked."

"There is no human history in the world, I suppose," said Don Quixote, "that has not its ups and downs — but more than others, those that deal with chivalry, since they can never be made up entirely of prosperous adventures."

"For all that," replied the bachelor, "there are those who have read the history who say they would have been glad if the author had left out some of the countless cudgellings inflicted on Señor Don Quixote in his various encounters."
"That's where the truth of the history comes in," said Sancho.

"At the same time, they might fairly have passed them over in silence," observed Don Quixote; "for there is no need to record events that do not change or affect the truth of a history, if they tend to bring the hero of it into contempt. Aeneas was not in truth and earnest as pious as Virgil represents him, nor Ulysses as wise as Homer describes him."

"That is true," said Samson; "but it is one thing to write as a poet, another to write as a historian. The poet may describe or sing things not as they were, but as they ought to have been; but the historian has to write them down not as they ought to have been, but as they were, without adding anything to the truth or taking anything from it."

"Well then," said Sancho, "if this señor Moor goes in for telling the truth, no doubt among my master's drubbings mine are to be found; for they never took the measure of his worship's shoulders without doing the same for my whole body. But I've no right to wonder at that, for, as my master himself says, the members must share the pain of the head."
"You are a sly dog, Sancho," said Don Quixote; "upon my faith, you have no want of memory when you choose to remember."
"If I tried to forget the thwacks they gave me," said Sancho, "my weals would not let me; they're still fresh on my ribs."
"Hush, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and don't interrupt the bachelor, whom I entreat to go on and tell all that is said about me in this history."
"And about me," said Sancho, "for they say, too, that I'm one of the principal presonages in it."
"Personages, not presonages, friend Sancho," said Samson.
"What! Another word-catcher!" said Sancho. "If that's to be the way, we shan't make an end in a lifetime."

"May God shorten mine, Sancho," returned the bachelor, "if you are not the second person in the history; and there are some who would rather hear you talk than the cleverest in the whole book — though there are some, too, who say you showed yourself over-credulous in believing there was any possibility in the government of that island offered you by Señor Don Quixote."

"There is still sunshine on the wall," said Don Quixote; "and when Sancho is somewhat more advanced in life, with the experience that years bring, he will be fitter and better qualified to be a governor than he is at present."

"By God, master," said Sancho, "the island that I can't govern with the years I have, I'll not be able to govern with the years of Methuselah. The trouble is that the said island keeps its distance somewhere — I know not where — and not that there's any want of head in me to govern it."
"Leave it to God, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "for all will be, and perhaps better than you think; no leaf on the tree stirs but by God's will."
"That's true," said Samson; "and if it is God's will, there won't be any want of a thousand islands, much less one, for Sancho to govern."
"I've seen governors in these parts," said Sancho, "who are not to be compared to my shoe-sole; and for all that, they're called 'your lordship' and served on silver."
"Those are not governors of islands," observed Samson, "but of other governments of an easier kind: those who govern islands must at least know grammar."

"I could manage the gram well enough," said Sancho, "but for the mar I have neither leaning nor liking, for I don't know what it is. But, leaving this matter of the government in God's hands to send me wherever it may be most to his service, I may tell you, señor bachelor Samson Carrasco, that it has pleased me beyond measure that the author of this history should have spoken of me in such a way that what is said of me gives no offence; for, on the faith of a true squire, if he had said anything about me that was at all unbecoming an old Christian like myself, the deaf would have heard of it."
"That would be working miracles," said Samson.
"Miracles or no miracles," said Sancho, "let everyone mind how he speaks or writes about people, and not set down at random the first thing that comes into his head."

"One of the faults they find with this history," said the bachelor, "is that its author inserted in it a novella called 'The Ill-Advised Curiosity' — not that it is bad or ill-told, but that it is out of place and has nothing to do with the history of his worship Señor Don Quixote."
"I'll bet the son of a dog has mixed the cabbages and the baskets," said Sancho.

"Then I say," said Don Quixote, "the author of my history was no sage, but some ignorant chatterer who, in a haphazard and heedless way, set about writing it, let it turn out as it might — just as Orbaneja, the painter of Úbeda, used to do, who, when they asked him what he was painting, answered, 'Whatever it turns out.' Sometimes he would paint a cock in such a fashion, and so unlike one, that he had to write alongside it in Gothic letters, 'This is a cock.' And so it will be with my history, which will need a commentary to make it intelligible."

"No fear of that," returned Samson, "for it is so plain that there's nothing in it to puzzle over. The children turn its leaves, the young people read it, the grown men understand it, the old folk praise it; in a word, the book is so thumbed, so read, and so committed to memory by people of every sort, that the instant they see any lean hack they say, 'There goes Rocinante.' And those most given to reading it are the pages; for there is not a lord's antechamber where a 'Don Quixote' is not to be found — one takes it up if another lays it down, this one pounces on it, that one begs for it. In short, the said history is the most delightful and least injurious entertainment yet seen, for there isn't to be found in the whole of it even the semblance of an immodest word or a thought that is anything but Catholic."

"To write in any other way," said Don Quixote, "would not be to write truth, but falsehood; and historians who have recourse to falsehood ought to be burned, like those who coin false money. I don't know what could have led the author to have recourse to novellas and irrelevant stories, when he had so much to write about in mine; no doubt he must have gone by the proverb 'with straw or with hay, &c.,' for by merely setting forth my thoughts, my sighs, my tears, my lofty purposes, my enterprises, he could have made a volume as large, or larger, than all the works of El Tostado put together. The conclusion I arrive at, señor bachelor, is that to write histories, or books of any kind, requires great judgment and a ripe understanding. To give expression to humour and write in a strain of graceful pleasantry is the gift of great geniuses. The cleverest character in comedy is the clown, for the man who would make people take him for a fool must not be one. History is in a measure a sacred thing, for it should be true, and where the truth is, there God is; but, all the same, there are some who write and fling books broadcast on the world as if they were fritters."
"There is no book so bad but it has something good in it," said the bachelor.

"No doubt of that," replied Don Quixote; "but it often happens that those who have acquired and attained a well-deserved reputation by their writings lose it entirely, or damage it in some degree, when they give them to the press."

"The reason for that," said Samson, "is that, since printed works are examined at leisure, their faults are easily seen; and the greater the fame of the writer, the more closely are they scrutinised. Men famous for their genius — great poets, illustrious historians — are always, or most commonly, envied by those who take a particular delight and pleasure in criticising the writings of others without having produced any of their own."
"That is no wonder," said Don Quixote; "for there are many divines who are no good for the pulpit, but excellent at detecting the defects or excesses of those who preach."

"All that is true, Señor Don Quixote," said Carrasco, "but I wish such fault-finders were more lenient and less exacting, and did not pay so much attention to the spots on the bright sun of the work they grumble at; for if _aliquando bonus dormitat Homerus_, they should remember how long he remained awake to shed the light of his work with as little shade as possible. And perhaps it may be that what they find fault with may be moles, that sometimes heighten the beauty of the face that bears them. And so I say very great is the risk to which a man who prints a book exposes himself, for of all impossibilities the greatest is to write one that will satisfy and please all readers."
"That which treats of me must have pleased few," said Don Quixote.

"Quite the contrary," said the bachelor; "for, as _stultorum infinitum est numerus_, innumerable are those who have relished the said history; but some have brought a charge against the author's memory, in that he forgot to say who the thief was who stole Sancho's Dapple — for it is not stated there, but only to be inferred from what is set down, that it was stolen; and a little further on we see Sancho mounted on the same ass, without any reappearance of it. They say, too, that he forgot to state what Sancho did with those hundred crowns he found in the valise in the Sierra Morena, since he never alludes to them again; and there are many who would be glad to know what he did with them, or what he spent them on — for it is one of the serious omissions of the work."

"Señor Samson, I'm not in a humour now for going into accounts or explanations," said Sancho; "for I have a sinking in my stomach, and unless I doctor it with a couple of sips of the old stuff, it will put me on the thorn of Santa Lucia. I have it at home, and my old woman is waiting for me; after dinner I'll come back, and will answer you and all the world every question you choose to ask, as well about the loss of the ass as about the spending of the hundred crowns." And without another word or waiting for a reply, he made off home.

Don Quixote begged and entreated the bachelor to stay and do penance with him. The bachelor accepted the invitation and remained; a couple of young pigeons were added to the ordinary fare; at dinner they talked chivalry; Carrasco fell in with his host's humour; the banquet came to an end; they took their afternoon sleep; Sancho returned; and their conversation was resumed.
